advisories.description:
### Summary

When an issue or pull request is locked, Gitea is supposed to stop people who aren't collaborators from interacting with the thread. The API does enforce this for reactions — it returns 403. But the two web handlers that add and remove reactions never check whether the issue is locked, so the same action goes through when it's sent to the web routes.

The practical result: any signed-in user who can see a locked thread (including a complete stranger on a public repo) can keep adding or removing emoji reactions on it from the web UI, even though a maintainer locked it to stop exactly that.

This is a moderation gap, not a data-exposure or privilege-escalation bug. I'd rate it Low severity.

### Details

Vulnerability type
Incorrect authorization / missing access check (CWE-285). Inconsistent enforcement between API and web layers.

Description
When an issue or pull request is locked, Gitea should stop non-collaborators from interacting with the thread. The API enforces this for reactions and returns 403. The two web handlers that add/remove reactions never check whether the issue is locked, so the same action succeeds when sent to the web routes. Any signed-in user who can view a locked thread (on a public repo, effectively anyone) can add or remove reactions on it through the web UI.

Affected code

routers/web/repo/issue.go — ChangeIssueReaction (~line 485): no lock check
routers/web/repo/issue_comment.go — ChangeCommentReaction: no lock check
routers/web/web.go (~lines 1378, 1405): these routes aren’t covered by the MustAllowUserComment middleware that guards the new-comment route (~line 1367)
Correct reference: routers/api/v1/repo/issue_reaction.go (~lines 208, 423) checks IsLocked && !CanWriteIssuesOrPulls && !IsAdmin and returns 403

### Impact

Impact
Anyone signed in who can view a locked issue, PR, or comment — which on a public repo is everyone — can add or remove reactions on it via the web UI, bypassing the lock. The main real-world effect is being able to pile reactions onto a thread a maintainer deliberately locked (for example a heated discussion).

No information is exposed and no permissions are gained.

Suggested fix

Add the same check the API already uses to both web handlers, or better, move it into the shared reaction service (services/issue/reaction.go) so the API and web paths can't drift apart again. Roughly:

go
if issue.IsLocked && !ctx.Repo.Permission.CanWriteIssuesOrPulls(issue.IsPull) {
    ctx.HTTPError(http.StatusForbidden)
    return
}
advisories.summary: Locked issues and comments still accept reactions through the web UI

advisories.description:
### Summary

Gitea protects state-changing web routes against cross-site requests in `crossOriginProtection.Check` (`web.go:218-223`). That check runs inside the sign-in middleware (`verifyAuthWithOptionsWeb`, through `reqSignIn`/`optSignIn`).

The repository-topics route is registered in a group with `context.RepoAssignment, reqRepoAdmin` but **without** any sign-in middleware. The cross-origin check therefore never runs, so a cross-site POST carrying the victim's session cookie is accepted. Sibling routes such as `/action/star` are correctly rejected with 403.

### Details

the source location should be routers/web/web.go:1524-1526

### Impact

- A malicious or compromised website can silently overwrite or clear the topics of any repository whose admin visits it while logged in to Gitea.
- This enables defacement, misleading search and discovery results (for example tagging a repo as "malware" or adding SEO spam), and wiping curated topic sets.
- The impact is limited to integrity of the topics field, with no data disclosure.
advisories.summary: Cross-Site Request Forgery on `POST /{owner}/{repo}/topics`

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

advisories.description:
### Summary

Draft releases leak instance-wide attachment metadata (file names, UUIDs, upload timestamps, sizes, download counts) from private repositories and abandoned uploads to any user who can create a draft release.

### Details

> [!NOTE]
> I'm not a security researcher; I'm an open source maintainer - you can find out more about me at https://roe.dev.
>
> I've been building an open-source cross-forge TypeScript client (https://github.com/danielroe/forges - or see https://forges.link) to help developers write code that 'just works' across different forges (I'd love to make sure it works really well with Gitea!). Part of the validation process is recording API responses from different code forges to make sure that the client handles it correctly.
>
> While recording the response from creating a draft release, I discovered a vulnerability because the response was vastly more than I expected.

Specifically, creating a draft release through the API returns an `assets` array with metadata for attachments belonging to the whole instance. The array holds issue and comment attachments from repositories the caller cannot read.

Call path, with functions on `main` at `c30ddc3e`:

1. `routers/api/v1/repo/release.go`, `CreateRelease()`: calls `release_service.CreateRelease()`, then returns `convert.ToAPIRelease()` for the same `rel`.
2. `services/release/release.go`, `CreateRelease()` (line ~172): calls `createTag()` before `db.Insert()`.
3. `services/release/release.go`, `createTag()` (line 69): calls `rel.LoadAttributes(ctx)` unconditionally. At this point `rel.ID` is `0`, since the row is not inserted until line 188.
4. `models/repo/release.go`, `LoadAttributes()`: calls `GetReleaseAttachments()`.
5. `models/repo/release.go`, `GetReleaseAttachments()` (line 411): runs `In("release_id", sortedRels.ID)` with no repository filter. For an unsaved release that is `release_id IN (0)`. Issue and comment attachments are stored with `release_id = 0`, so every such attachment on the instance matches.
6. `services/convert/release.go`, `ToAPIRelease()`: sets `Attachments: ToAPIAttachments(ctx, repo, r.Attachments)`, so the matched rows are returned.

Verified response from a local `28.1.0` instance (the file belongs to a private repository the caller cannot read):

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "tag_name": "draft-test",
  "draft": true,
  "assets": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "victim-private-plan.txt",
      "size": 16,
      "download_count": 0,
      "created_at": "2026-10-10T13:59:17Z",
      "uuid": "5429f66e-1ddb-4409-b17e-bc633d18e7d7",
      "browser_download_url": "http://127.0.0.1:3000/outsider/own-repo/releases/download/draft-test/victim-private-plan.txt"
    }
  ]
}
```

Note that the `browser_download_url` is rewritten to the attacker's own repository, and it 404s when fetched, as do `/attachments/<uuid>` and the API asset route, so the leak is metadata only.

Why published releases look fine (verified live: they return an empty `assets` array, as does a `PATCH` of the draft): `services/notify`'s `NewRelease()` calls `rel.LoadAttributes()` again after the insert, which resets `Attachments` to the correct empty set before the response is built. Drafts never reach that notifier, so the polluted list survives.

This was introduced by commit `28f9b313b` (2023-09-22, "Updates to the API for archived repos", #27149), which moved `LoadAttributes()` to the top of `createTag()` so `rel.Repo.MustNotBeArchived()` could run. Commit `882e50232` later touched the same line. Both are in `v1.22.0`.

### Impact

- **Type:** information exposure through an API response (metadata only).
- **Who is affected:** any Gitea instance on `v1.22.0` or later, plus `main`. Exposure is limited to accounts that can create a draft release, which in practice means any registered user with a repository.
- **What leaks:** for each attachment on the instance with no release link (issue and comment uploads, and uploads that were never posted to an issue), its name, UUID, size, timestamps and download count. This includes attachments from private repositories.
- **What does not leak:** file contents. `/attachments/<uuid>`, the API asset route, and the `browser_download_url` in the response all return 404 for the attacker and for anonymous requests.
- **Scale:** when recording API fixtures for https://github.com/danielroe/forges on public instances: about 8,000 entries were leaked from gitea.com and about 148,000 (roughly 41 MB) were leaked on Codeberg, in respnose to one request.
advisories.summary: Draft releases include attachment metadata from other repositories

advisories.description:
### Summary

`DeleteLabel(ctx, id, labelID)` takes one untyped `id` and compares it against the
label's org id *or* its repo id, depending on what kind of label it turns out to be.
Repository ids and organisation ids come from independent sequences and collide freely.
A user with issues-write on repository id *N* can therefore delete labels belonging to
organisation id *N*, a tenant they have no standing in.

### Details
```go
// models/issues/label.go:273-302 (v1.27.3)
func DeleteLabel(ctx context.Context, id, labelID int64) error {
	l, err := GetLabelByID(ctx, labelID)
	…
	return db.WithTx(ctx, func(ctx context.Context) error {
		if l.BelongsToOrg() && l.OrgID != id {
			return nil
		}
		if l.BelongsToRepo() && l.RepoID != id {
			return nil
		}

		if _, err = db.DeleteByID[Label](ctx, labelID); err != nil {
			…
```

Which test runs is chosen by the *label's* kind, not the caller's. The repo-scoped
handler passes `ctx.Repo.Repository.ID`; if `labelID` resolves to an **org** label, the
first branch compares that repository id against the label's organisation id. Equal
numbers pass the check and the delete goes ahead.

Callers: `routers/api/v1/repo/label.go:271`, `routers/api/v1/org/label.go:252`,
`routers/web/repo/issue_label.go:157`, `routers/web/org/org_labels.go:88`. The org-side
routes require `reqOrgOwnership`; the repo-side ones do not.

### Impact

This deletes one tenant's labels from inside another tenant. Labels carry triage state,
so removing an organisation's labels detaches them from every issue in that org that
used them. The collision is not attacker-chosen. My run arranges one deliberately with
filler repositories on an empty instance; on a populated instance, forcing a *specific*
collision may well be impractical, though spotting an existing one is cheap since both
ids are visible through the API. I scored `AC:H` for that, and I have shown the missing
type check rather than a practical targeted attack.

CVE-2026-58445 (`GHSA-pgqf-926r-548m`) and CVE-2026-25038 fixed label scoping at or
below 1.27.0; this conflation survives both.

### AI usage

I noticed `DeleteLabel` scopes on a single untyped id, read that function and its four
callers at `v1.27.3`, then ran the colliding-id fixture against both routes on a private
instance; the PoC block is its stdout. An LLM helped with the prose.
advisories.summary: DeleteLabel compares one untyped id against whichever namespace the label uses, letting a repo collaborator delete an ID-colliding organisation's labels

advisories.description:
### Summary

`attachmentBelongsToRepoOrIssue` validates that an attachment belongs to the right
repository and the right issue, but never checks `CommentID`. The issue-scoped routes
therefore accept an attachment id that belongs to a *comment* on that issue. A user
whose only relationship to the repository is opening an issue can delete or rename an
attachment posted by someone else in a comment.

### Details

The check covers two of the three scopes it needs:

```go
// routers/api/v1/repo/issue_attachment.go:383-399 (v1.27.3)
func attachmentBelongsToRepoOrIssue(ctx *context.APIContext, attachment *repo_model.Attachment, issue *issues_model.Issue) bool {
	if attachment.RepoID != ctx.Repo.Repository.ID {
		…
		return false
	}
	if attachment.IssueID == 0 {
		…
		return false
	} else if issue != nil && attachment.IssueID != issue.ID {
		…
		return false
	}
	return true
}
```

A comment attachment has a non-zero `IssueID`, so it passes all three tests. The sibling
check, `attachmentBelongsToRepoOrComment`, does require `CommentID != 0`. The two route
families authorise differently:

- issue-scoped: `doer == issue.PosterID` **OR** `CanWriteIssuesOrPulls`
- comment-scoped: `doer == comment.PosterID` **AND** `CanWriteIssuesOrPulls`

Both also admit repo and site admins; the issue opener satisfies the first.

The same scoping omission, a delete that resolves an object id without checking the
parent named in the URL, was fixed in 1.25.5 as CVE-2026-25782
(`GHSA-qm72-8prh-g92x`); this is the issue-attachment instance of it.

### Impact

Any user who opens an issue can delete or rename attachments other participants post
in comments on it, with no repository permission and no notice to the owner. It
reaches only issues the attacker opened, and adding to or editing another user's
comment is refused with 403. PATCH changes the filename, never the bytes, so this is
not XSS and not content replacement.

### AI usage

I noticed that the two checks test different things. I confirmed both, and the two
authorisation rules, at `v1.27.3`, then built the three-party fixture and ran it in
Docker here; the PoC section is that run's output. I used an LLM while writing this up.
advisories.summary: Issue-scoped attachment routes accept comment-scoped attachment ids, letting an issue opener delete or rename other users' comment attachments

cwes.name: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

advisories.description:
### Summary

Two web routes end in one private handler. `POST /releases/delete` requires
`reqRepoReleaseWriter` (`unit.TypeReleases`); `POST /{owner}/{repo}/tags/delete`
requires only `reqRepoCodeWriter` (`unit.TypeCode`). Neither the lookup nor the delete
tells a bare tag from a full release, so a collaborator with only **Code:Write** can
permanently destroy a release row and every attachment, in the database and in blob
storage.

### Details
```go
// routers/web/web.go:1478-1480 (v1.27.3)
		}, ctxDataSet("EnableFeed", setting.Other.EnableFeed))
		m.Post("/tags/delete", reqSignIn, reqRepoCodeWriter, context.RepoMustNotBeArchived(), repo.DeleteTag)
	}, optSignIn, context.RepoAssignment, repo.MustBeNotEmpty, reqUnitCodeReader)
```

`repo.DeleteTag` calls `deleteReleaseOrTag(ctx, true)`, the same function
`repo.DeleteRelease` calls with `false`. The lookup keys on `(id, repo_id)`, with no
`IsTag` filter:

```go
// models/repo/release.go:244-248 (v1.27.3)
func GetReleaseForRepoByID(ctx context.Context, repoID, id int64) (*Release, error) {
	rel := new(Release)
	has, err := db.GetEngine(ctx).
		Where("id=? AND repo_id=?", id, repoID).
		Get(rel)
```

`DeleteReleaseByID` branches on the caller-supplied `delTag`; it never reads
`rel.IsTag`. The REST API makes the check this route skips:

```go
// routers/api/v1/repo/tag.go:280-283 (v1.27.3)
	if !tag.IsTag {
		ctx.APIError(http.StatusConflict, "a tag attached to a release cannot be deleted directly")
		return
	}
```

`PushUpdateDeleteTags` (`models/repo/release.go:449-476`) deletes only `is_tag = true`
rows, so `git push origin :refs/tags/v1.0.0` leaves the release row and its attachment
alive. This route bypasses that protection. The UI check on `$release.IsTag`
(`templates/repo/tag/list.tmpl:45`) is client-side only.

GHSA-q423-49rw-g9mh was the same shape: a fix that landed on one route and not on the
route beside it.

### Impact

An account with Code:Write and no Releases:Write can permanently delete published
releases and their binaries. Scope is one repository: another repo's release id returns
404 and leaves that release untouched. A `tag_protection` pattern that covers the tag
and does not allowlist the caller stops it, since `DeleteReleaseByID` checks protected
tags before deleting anything (`services/release/release.go:366-378`), but that
protection is off by default and set per repository.

CVE-2025-68938 (`GHSA-cm54-pfmc-xrwx`), "Gitea mishandles authorization for deletion of
releases", fixed in 1.25.2, is a different route in the same area and not this.

### AI usage

I found this by noticing two routes reach one handler, confirmed the missing `IsTag`
filter at `v1.27.3`, then reproduced it in a local lab; the PoC transcript is that run.
I had help from an LLM writing it.
advisories.summary: POST /{owner}/{repo}/tags/delete requires only Code:Write but destroys Releases and their attachment blobs

advisories.description:
## Summary

The `GET /api/v1/user/subscriptions` endpoint in Gitea returns full repository metadata for every watched (subscribed) repository without verifying that the authenticated caller still has access. After an organization administrator downgrades a team's permissions, a former collaborator who watched a private repository while they had access can still retrieve its metadata (name, description, visibility, clone URLs, owner, branch count, issue/PR counts, topics, and other properties) through this endpoint.

## Root Cause

`getWatchedRepos` in `routers/api/v1/user/watch.go` computes a per-repository permission object via `GetIndividualUserRepoPermission` but never evaluates it as an access gate. The permission object is passed to `convert.ToRepo` for formatting only. No `HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()` check exists in this function.

```go
// watch.go:34-41 (vulnerable)
repos := make([]*api.Repository, len(watchedRepos))
for i, watched := range watchedRepos {
    permission, err := access_model.GetIndividualUserRepoPermission(ctx, watched, user)
    if err != nil { return nil, 0, err }
    repos[i] = convert.ToRepo(ctx, watched, permission)  // no access gate
}
```

The fixed sibling function `getStarredRepos` in `routers/api/v1/user/star.go` demonstrates the intended pattern: it uses `make(0, len)` with conditional `append`, skipping repositories where `!permission.HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()`. The watched-repos function uses `make(len)` with direct index assignment, structurally unable to skip entries.

The SQL-level `AccessibleRepositoryCondition` applied in `WatchedReposOptions.ToConds()` uses `UserOrgTeamRepoCond` (when `unitType == unit.TypeInvalid`), which only checks that `team_user` and `team_repo` rows exist. It does not join on `team.authorize` or `team_unit.access_mode`, so it matches after team permission downgrade as long as the user remains a team member. Additionally, `UpdateTeam` in `services/org/team.go` calls `RecalculateTeamAccesses` but not `ReconsiderWatches`, leaving watch entries orphaned after permission changes.

## Impact

An authenticated user whose organization team-based access to a private repository was downgraded can read the repository's full metadata by calling `GET /api/v1/user/subscriptions` with a user-scoped token. The user must have watched the repository while they had access; after the team's permissions are downgraded via `PATCH /api/v1/teams/{id}`, the watch entry persists and the SQL filter's `UserOrgTeamRepoCond` branch continues to match.

Disclosed metadata includes: repository name, full path, description, visibility flag, clone URLs (HTTPS and SSH), HTML URL, owner information, default branch, size, stars/forks/watchers counts, branch count, open issue and PR counts, release count, topics, licenses, and timestamps. No repository content (source code, issue bodies, pull request text, comments, commits, or secrets) is disclosed. Clone URLs are returned but are not usable without separate access.

## Affected Versions

- Ecosystem: Go
- Package: `code.gitea.io/gitea`
- Confirmed affected range: `<= 1.27.3`
- Latest release checked: v1.27.3 (published 2026-08-29, confirmed via `git show v1.27.3:routers/api/v1/user/watch.go`)
- Fix status: not fixed in any published version

The `getWatchedRepos` function has never contained the `HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()` filter in any version. The vulnerability predates the CVE-2026-59766 fix (v1.27.0) and persists through v1.27.3. The introduction version cannot be precisely determined from the available checkout, but the function structure (fixed-size allocation with index assignment rather than conditional append) indicates the filter was never present.

## Suggested Fix

Add the `HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()` check to `getWatchedRepos` in `routers/api/v1/user/watch.go`, following the pattern established in `getStarredRepos`: change the allocation to `make([]*api.Repository, 0, len(watchedRepos))`, check `permission.HasAnyUnitAccessOrPublicAccess()` for each repository, and use `append` to include only accessible repositories.

Additionally, call `ReconsiderWatches` from `UpdateTeam` when `authChanged=true` to clean up orphaned watch entries, consistent with the existing `removeTeamMember` behavior. Consider also using the stricter `userOrgTeamUnitRepoBuilder` (which checks `team.authorize` and `team_unit.access_mode`) in `AccessibleRepositoryCondition` when `unitType == unit.TypeInvalid`, as a defense-in-depth measure for any future endpoints that may query repositories via team membership.

No interim mitigation is available without a code change. Administrators can remove users from teams (which triggers `ReconsiderWatches`) rather than downgrading team permissions to ensure watch entries are cleaned up.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
advisories.summary: Gitea watched-repos API (GET /api/v1/user/subscriptions) leaks private repository metadata after team permission downgrade

advisories.description:
## Summary

Gitea's `AddReleaseAttachments` function accepts attachment UUIDs without verifying that each attachment is not already linked to an issue. An authenticated user with release write permission can re-link an issue-bound attachment to a release they control, exposing attachment metadata (filename, size, download count) through the release page and API, and enabling permanent deletion or renaming of the targeted issue attachment.

## Root Cause

The CVE-2026-57886 fix introduced `validateAttachmentForIssue` to reject attachments already linked to another issue or to a release. This validation is applied to `UpdateIssueAttachments` and `UpdateCommentAttachments`, but the release counterpart `AddReleaseAttachments` was not updated with a symmetric `IssueID` check.

```text
Affected function: AddReleaseAttachments
Location: models/repo/release.go (line 181)

The function checks:
  - attachments[i].RepoID != rel.RepoID  (rejects cross-repo)
  - attachments[i].ReleaseID != 0        (rejects already-linked-to-release)

Missing check:
  - attachments[i].IssueID != 0          (does NOT reject already-linked-to-issue)

Compare with validateAttachmentForIssue (models/issues/issue_update.go:269):
  - attachment.RepoID != issue.RepoID     (rejects cross-repo)
  - attachment.IssueID != 0 && ...        (rejects already-linked-to-another-issue)
  - attachment.ReleaseID != 0             (rejects already-linked-to-release)
```

## Impact

An authenticated attacker with write access to the Releases unit in a repository can target any issue attachment in the same repository whose UUID is known. Gitea's unit-level team permissions support granting release write without issue access; this is a non-default but supported configuration. The attack requires knowledge of a target attachment UUID, which may leak through notification emails, webhook payloads, RSS/Atom feeds, browser history, or Markdown content viewed before permission changes. UUID enumeration is infeasible (v4, 128-bit random).

After re-linking, the attacker can:

- **Disclose metadata:** The attachment's filename, UUID, size, and download count appear in the release's attachment list (web page and API endpoint `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/{id}/assets`). Filenames may contain sensitive information.
- **Rename the attachment:** The release edit interface allows changing the attachment's display name.
- **Permanently delete the attachment:** The release edit interface can remove the attachment, deleting both the database record and the physical file from storage. The re-link and deletion can occur in a single HTTP request.

File content download is independently protected: `GetAttachmentLinkedTypeAndRepoID` checks `IssueID` before `ReleaseID`, so the download handler verifies issue-level read permission on the original repository. An attacker without issue read access cannot download the file content.

## Affected Versions

- Ecosystem: Go
- Package: `code.gitea.io/gitea`
- Confirmed affected range: `<= 1.27.3`
- Latest release checked: v1.27.3 (GitHub Releases, published 2026-08-29)
- Fix status: not fixed in any published version

The `AddReleaseAttachments` function has contained the same validation gap since before the CVE-2026-57886 fix was applied. The introduction boundary predates the available git history and cannot be precisely determined. The current `go.mod` module path is `gitea.dev`, but the established advisory package coordinate is `code.gitea.io/gitea`.

## Suggested Fix

Add an `IssueID` check to `AddReleaseAttachments` in `models/repo/release.go`, symmetric with the existing `ReleaseID` check in `validateAttachmentForIssue`. Specifically, after the existing `ReleaseID != 0` check, reject any attachment where `IssueID != 0`:

```go
if attachments[i].IssueID != 0 {
    return util.NewPermissionDeniedErrorf("attachment is already linked to an issue")
}
```

This prevents issue-bound attachments from being re-linked to releases. The same check should be added to any future attachment linking function. Consider also verifying that the attachment was uploaded by the current user or belongs to the current session.

No interim mitigation is available beyond restricting the Releases write permission to users who also hold issue access in the same repository.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
advisories.summary: Gitea AddReleaseAttachments missing IssueID check allows issue attachment metadata exposure and deletion via releases

advisories.description:
## Summary

The `hookPostReceiveUpdateRepoByOptions` function in Gitea's post-receive hook handler processes `repo.private` push options on empty repositories without checking the `setting.Repository.ForcePrivate` server policy. On instances where ForcePrivate is enabled, any authenticated user with repository admin permission (including regular repo creators) can make a repository public via `git push -o repo.private=false`, bypassing the site-level policy that every other visibility-change path enforces.

## Root Cause

The ForcePrivate server policy is a site-level configuration (`FORCE_PRIVATE = true` in `app.ini`) intended to prevent non-site-admin users from making repositories public. Every visibility-change path in Gitea enforces this policy except the push option handler.

```text
Affected function: hookPostReceiveUpdateRepoByOptions
File: routers/private/hook_post_receive.go (lines 143-188 in v1.27.3)

The function checks ctx.Repo.Permission.IsAdmin() (repo-level) at line 159
and repo.IsEmpty at line 166, but never checks setting.Repository.ForcePrivate.

Comparison with other paths that DO enforce the policy:
- API Edit: routers/api/v1/repo/repo.go line 696 checks ForcePrivate && !ctx.Doer.IsAdmin
- Web UI Settings: routers/web/repo/setting/setting.go line 1077 checks ForcePrivate && !ctx.Doer.IsAdmin
- Public Access: routers/web/repo/setting/public_access.go line 30 checks ForcePrivate
- Push-to-create service: services/repository/repository.go line 101 applies ForcePrivate at creation
```

## Impact

When `FORCE_PRIVATE = true` is configured (a non-default, enterprise-oriented security setting), any authenticated user who can create repositories can bypass the policy on the push-to-create path. The repository is correctly created as private (the creation path enforces ForcePrivate), but the subsequent push option flips visibility to public. This makes the repository and its contents accessible to unauthenticated users, violating the organizational policy that all repositories must remain private.

The attacker must be an authenticated user with repository admin permission. Since all repository creators are automatically admins of their own repos, this is equivalent to any registered user. The attacker controls what content they push, so the confidentiality impact is limited to their own data becoming publicly visible in violation of policy. The integrity impact is the unauthorized modification of a security-relevant repository attribute.

ForcePrivate defaults to `false`, so only instances that have explicitly enabled this security policy are affected.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An authenticated user pushes to an empty Gitea repository over HTTP or SSH. The post-receive hook fires for all pushes, including push-to-create.
2. **Control:** The attacker includes `-o repo.private=false` as a push option. This value is read as a boolean at `hook_post_receive.go:144` and directly controls the `isPrivate` variable.
3. **Path:** The push option is forwarded via the internal API to `hookPostReceiveUpdateRepoByOptions`. The function loads the repo, checks repo-level admin permission (line 159), and checks `repo.IsEmpty` (line 166). For a first push to an empty repo, both checks pass.
4. **Guard:** The missing check is `setting.Repository.ForcePrivate`. Unlike the API edit endpoint (`repo.go:696`) and the web UI settings endpoint (`setting.go:1077`), the push option handler does not check this server-level policy before allowing a private-to-public transition.
5. **Primitive:** `repo.IsPrivate = isPrivate.Value()` at line 173, persisted via `UpdateRepositoryColsNoAutoTime` at line 175. The database record changes the repository's visibility.
6. **Result:** The repository becomes publicly accessible. Anonymous users receive `AccessModeRead` permission because `GetIndividualUserRepoPermission` at `repo_permission.go:466` grants read access when `repo.IsPrivate` is false and the user is nil (unauthenticated).

## Bypass Evidence

This finding is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-58437 (GHSA-8p9h-49rc-qgxj). The CVE fix added a `!repo.IsEmpty` guard at line 166 to restrict push options to empty repositories only, preventing visibility manipulation on populated repos. However, the fix did not add `ForcePrivate` enforcement on the remaining allowed path (empty repos during push-to-create).

The push option handler at `hook_post_receive.go` contains zero references to `setting.Repository.ForcePrivate`, `ForcePrivate`, or `ctx.Doer.IsAdmin`. This was confirmed by searching the entire file. Every other code path that changes repository visibility (API edit, web UI settings, public access settings) enforces the ForcePrivate policy by checking `setting.Repository.ForcePrivate && !ctx.Doer.IsAdmin` before allowing a private-to-public transition.

The strongest disproof attempted was whether `applyPublicAccessPermission` in the permission model provides a runtime backstop when ForcePrivate is enabled. Investigation showed it only controls per-unit `anonymousAccessMode`, not the primary `perm.AccessMode` which is set to `AccessModeRead` at `repo_permission.go:466` when `IsPrivate=false`. No middleware-level ForcePrivate enforcement exists.

## Affected Versions

- Ecosystem: Go
- Package: `code.gitea.io/gitea`
- Confirmed affected range: `>= 1.27.0, <= 1.27.3`
- Latest release checked: v1.27.3 (published 2026-08-29, Go module proxy)
- Fix status: not fixed

The lower bound is v1.27.0 because that release introduced the CVE-2026-58437 fix (`!repo.IsEmpty` guard) which made the ForcePrivate gap independently exploitable. Before v1.27.0, the broader CVE-2026-58437 vulnerability (push options on all repos) subsumed this specific policy bypass. The ForcePrivate gap was never addressed in any release through v1.27.3.

## Suggested Fix

Add a `ForcePrivate` check in `hookPostReceiveUpdateRepoByOptions` before allowing a private-to-public transition. The check should mirror the pattern used in the API edit endpoint: when `ForcePrivate` is enabled and the push option would make a private repo public, deny the change unless the pusher is a site admin (`ctx.Doer.IsAdmin`). This ensures the push option handler enforces the same server-level policy as all other visibility-change paths.

As an interim mitigation, administrators can disable push-to-create functionality (`ENABLE_PUSH_CREATE_USER = false` and `ENABLE_PUSH_CREATE_ORG = false` in `app.ini`) to eliminate the empty-repo push path. Existing empty repositories created via the API or web UI remain exploitable through first push until the code is patched.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
advisories.summary: Gitea push-to-create ignores ForcePrivate server policy, allowing non-admin users to publish repositories as public

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

advisories.description:
## Summary

The `parseProtobufBody` function in Gitea's Actions Artifact V4 API reads the entire HTTP request body into memory via `io.ReadAll` with no size limit. An authenticated user who can trigger a GitHub Actions workflow can use the resulting runner token to send an oversized request to any of the five Artifact Service endpoints, causing an unrecoverable out-of-memory process kill that takes down all Gitea services.

## Root Cause

The application fails to enforce a size limit on the HTTP request body before reading it into a heap-allocated byte slice. `io.ReadAll` grows its internal buffer by doubling until the Go runtime cannot allocate the next backing array, at which point `runtime.throw("out of memory")` terminates the entire process.

```go
// routers/api/actions/artifactsv4.go:293-306
func (r *artifactV4Routes) parseProtobufBody(ctx *ArtifactContext, req protoreflect.ProtoMessage) bool {
    body, err := io.ReadAll(ctx.Req.Body) // no LimitReader, no size check
    if err != nil {
        log.Error("Error decode request body: %v", err)
        ctx.HTTPError(http.StatusInternalServerError, "Error decode request body")
        return false
    }
    err = protojson.Unmarshal(body, req)
    // ...
}
```

Five POST endpoints call this function: `CreateArtifact` (line 324), `FinalizeArtifact` (line 479), `ListArtifacts` (line 605), `GetSignedArtifactURL` (line 664), and `DeleteArtifact` (line 729). All are registered under the `/twirp/github.actions.results.api.v1.ArtifactService/` prefix.

## Impact

An attacker needs an authenticated Gitea account with push access to any repository that has Actions enabled (the default) and a connected runner. By pushing a workflow file, the attacker obtains a valid Actions runner token. A single oversized HTTP POST to any Artifact Service endpoint forces the server to allocate the full body into heap memory, triggering a fatal out-of-memory condition. The resulting process kill affects all Gitea services (web UI, API, git operations, CI/CD, package registry) for all users. The server requires a manual restart and is immediately re-exploitable. Concurrent oversized requests can maintain a persistent denial of service even with automatic restart policies.

## Affected Versions

- Ecosystem: Go
- Package: `code.gitea.io/gitea`
- Confirmed affected range: `>= 1.22.0`
- Latest release checked: v1.27.3 (confirmed vulnerable; `io.ReadAll(ctx.Req.Body)` at line 295 with no `LimitReader`)
- Fix status: not fixed through v1.27.3; no commit has ever added a body size limit to `parseProtobufBody`

The vulnerable code was introduced in commit `a53d268aca` ("Actions Artifacts v4 backend (#28965)"), first included in the v1.22.0 release. The Go module path changed from `code.gitea.io/gitea` to `gitea.dev` starting with v1.27.0.

## Suggested Fix

Wrap `ctx.Req.Body` in `io.LimitReader` within `parseProtobufBody`, analogous to the existing pattern in `job_summary.go:55` and the CVE-2026-42931 fix in `npm.go:437`. A reasonable limit would be based on the maximum expected protobuf JSON body size for artifact metadata (likely under 64 KB). All five calling endpoints would be protected by a single change to `parseProtobufBody`.

As an interim mitigation, a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, Traefik) in front of Gitea can enforce a global request body size limit (for example, `client_max_body_size 10m` in nginx). However, this is a deployment-specific measure and does not address the application-level vulnerability.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).
advisories.summary: Gitea Actions Artifact V4 API: unbounded request body read in parseProtobufBody enables memory-exhaustion DoS

advisories.description:
### Summary
Gitea's REST endpoint `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/push_mirrors` only checks `setting.Mirror.Enabled`. It does **not** check `setting.Mirror.DisableNewPush`, although the equivalent Web handler (`handleSettingsPostPushMirrorAdd`) does. As a result, when a site administrator sets `[mirror] DISABLE_NEW_PUSH = true` to forbid the creation of new push mirrors, a repository administrator can still create one through the API and establish a persistent outbound push mirror.

### Details
- Route mounting (`src/routers/api/v1/api.go:1505-1511`): the `/push_mirrors` group is protected by `reqAdmin(), reqToken()`, and nested in the `/repos/{username}/{reponame}` group guarded by `repoAssignment(), checkTokenPublicOnly()` plus `tokenRequiresScopes(Repository)`. So the caller must hold repository-admin (owner or AccessMode=Admin collaborator) or site-admin rights with a `Repository`-scoped token.
- Handler (`src/routers/api/v1/repo/mirror.go:255 AddPushMirror`) checks only `setting.Mirror.Enabled` (`:289`) and then calls `CreatePushMirror` (`:295`).
- `CreatePushMirror` (`src/routers/api/v1/repo/mirror.go:344`) validates the interval and the remote address (`git.ParseRemoteAddr` + `migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed`, which blocks private/loopback by default), inserts a `push_mirror` row, and registers the git remote via `mirror_service.AddPushMirrorRemote` (`src/services/mirror/mirror_push.go:33`) → `git.ManagedRemoteAdd` / `ManagedConfigAdd` (`src/modules/git/remote_managed.go:22`, `src/modules/git/config_managed.go:13`). Subsequent syncs run `git push --mirror --force` to that remote.
- The Web handler (`src/routers/web/repo/setting/setting.go:490-497`) rejects the same action with `if setting.Mirror.DisableNewPush || repo.IsArchived { ctx.NotFound(nil); return }`. A repository-wide grep shows `DisableNewPush` is referenced only in `src/modules/setting/mirror.go` and this Web handler — never on the API path.

### Impact
An authenticated repository administrator can bypass a site-administrator security policy and create an outbound push mirror that automatically force-pushes the entire repository (all refs) to an attacker-controlled remote, either on each commit (`sync_on_commit=true`) or on a schedule. This is an unauthorized administrative action and a persistent, automatic data-exfiltration channel that survives revocation of the creator's access.
advisories.summary: Gitea push-mirror creation API does not enforce the site-wide DISABLE_NEW_PUSH policy

advisories.description: The OAuth refresh-token endpoint verifies a token’s signature and grant but does not check that its token kind is `KindRefreshToken`. An unexpired access token for the same client and grant can therefore be submitted as a refresh token to obtain new access and refresh tokens. This can extend access beyond the captured access token’s original lifetime. The endpoint should reject any token whose kind is not `KindRefreshToken`.
advisories.summary: OAuth access tokens can be exchanged as refresh tokens

cwes.name: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

advisories.description:
### Summary

When migrating from another Gitea instance, the downloader asks the source how
many items it returns per page and then uses that number as its loop
terminator. A source that answers `0` makes every paginated fetch loop forever,
appending to a slice that's never released.

The source URL is whatever the user starting the migration typed in, so that
number comes from a server the attacker owns.

Measured on a clean 1.27.3: one migration request took the server from 99MiB to
5,758MiB of anonymous memory in 90 seconds, still climbing linearly when I
stopped it. An earlier run of the same thing hit 7,983MiB at 120 seconds, having
served 931,524 release pages, about 7,700 requests a second.

Any account that can create a repository can do this. No admin rights.

### Details

`services/migrations/gitea_downloader.go`:

```go
maxPerPage := 10
apiConf, _, err := giteaClient.Settings.GetGlobalAPISettings(ctx)
if err != nil {
	log.Info("Unable to get global API settings. Ignoring these.")
}
if apiConf != nil {
	maxPerPage = apiConf.MaxResponseItems
}
```

The error gets logged and then ignored rather than returned, the guard is
`apiConf != nil` rather than `err == nil` so a response that failed to parse
still supplies the value, and nothing checks the result is above zero.

Every paginated loop in the file then ends the same way:

```
216:  if !g.pagination || len(ms) < g.maxPerPage {        // milestones
254:  if !g.pagination || len(ls) < g.maxPerPage {        // labels
342:  if !g.pagination || len(rl) < g.maxPerPage {        // releases
381:  if !g.pagination || len(reactions) < g.maxPerPage { // reactions
511:  if !g.pagination || len(comments) < g.maxPerPage {  // comments
710:  if len(prl) < g.maxPerPage {                        // pull requests
```

`len(x) < 0` is never true, so none of them break. Six loops, one cause.

The `ctx.Done()` check inside the loops looks like it saves you and doesn't. The
API handler runs the migration as:

```go
doLongTimeMigrate(graceful.GetManager().HammerContext(), ctx.Doer)
```

which is the forced-shutdown context, not the request context, so the migration
is detached from the client on purpose. Disconnecting does nothing. There's no
timeout on the migration task and none on the migration HTTP client either. It
ends when the process does.

One caveat I want to be upfront about, because it looks worse than it is:
the lab sets `ALLOW_LOCALNETWORKS=true`. That's only because the fake source
sits on a private IP, and you block those for migrations by default, quite
rightly. A real attacker puts the source on a public host and needs no such
setting. The bug has nothing to do with local networks.

### Impact

Availability. One ordinary authenticated request drives unbounded memory growth
at roughly 66MiB/s and a request flood at roughly 7,700/s toward the attacker's
host, and nothing in Gitea stops it: no page cap, no item cap, no task timeout,
no client timeout, and the cancellation check is wired to a context that only
fires on shutdown.

Worth adding that even with a sane `maxPerPage`, a hostile source can return one
item per page forever and still grow the slice linearly. The zero just removes
the need to bother.

### Reachability

The attacker hosts the fake source. It has to answer about five endpoints:
`/api/v1/version`, `/api/v1/settings/api`, the repo object, `/topics`, and
`/releases`, plus a git repo over dumb HTTP so the clone succeeds. All of that
is in the PoC.

### Fix

Key on the error, and refuse a nonsensical value:

```go
apiConf, _, err := giteaClient.Settings.GetGlobalAPISettings(ctx)
if err != nil {
	log.Info("Unable to get global API settings, using the default. Error: %v", err)
} else if apiConf != nil && apiConf.MaxResponseItems > 0 {
	maxPerPage = apiConf.MaxResponseItems
}
```

Belt and braces would also cap total pages or total items per collection, for
the one-item-per-page case above.

### Severity

Same as the two sibling migration advisories, since it's the same class and the
same impact:

```
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H   6.5 Medium
```

CWE-400 is what you used on both of those. CWE-835, Loop with Unreachable Exit
Condition, is the more specific one and fits exactly.

### Versions

`apiConf != nil` and the `len(x) < g.maxPerPage` terminator are in every tag I
checked: 1.17.0, 1.19.0, 1.21.0, 1.23.0, 1.25.0, 1.27.0 and 1.27.3. Five such
loops through 1.25, six from 1.27.0. Still there on `main` at 9ae7ea7.

### Stuff I checked first

GHSA-5952-x23q-p23f (GitLab migration, uncancelable version probe) and
GHSA-46px-6cqx-c5fv (OneDev migration, unbounded version response body). Same
class, a hostile migration source exhausting the importer, fixed one downloader
at a time. The OneDev fix added `maxOneDevVersionResponseSize` and a
`LimitReader`, and that constant is still the only `LimitReader` anywhere in
`services/migrations`. The Gitea downloader never got looked at.

I also chased and dropped a second candidate in the same file, which you may
spot and wonder about: `gitea_downloader.go:302` builds the release asset
request with `http.NewRequest` and never attaches a context, while `gitlab.go:337`
attaches one on the next line. I built the hang and it survives client
disconnect, but so would anything, because of the `HammerContext` above. The
asymmetry is real but I couldn't show it has consequences beyond shutdown, so
I'm not reporting it as a vulnerability. Mentioning it in case it's worth
tidying.

### Credit

Dikshant Chandel (kewmine), Clickswave Labs Pvt Ltd.

Found during authorization research for Crossfyre (https://crossfyre.io). Same
method as the last couple: reading fix shapes rather than fuzzing. Two
advisories had hardened one migration downloader each against a hostile source,
and the single `LimitReader` they left behind made it obvious the other
downloaders had never been looked at with that threat in mind.

Happy to be credited as:

```
Dikshant Chandel (Clickswave Labs Pvt Ltd)
```
advisories.summary: A migration source reporting max_response_items: 0 makes six paginated loops in the Gitea downloader never terminate, exhausting server memory from one authenticated request

advisories.description:
### What happens

`GET /{username}/-/repositories` panics whenever the username belongs to an
individual user rather than an organization. No account needed, no setup, no
non-default configuration.

    anonymous  GET /solo/-/repositories     500  + panic in the log
    anonymous  GET /nosuch/-/repositories   404

### Why

`routers/web/org/home.go`:

    func Repositories(ctx *context.Context) {
        home(ctx, true)
    }

    func home(ctx *context.Context, viewRepositories bool) {
        org := ctx.Org.Organization        // nil when the context user is an individual

        ctx.Data["PageIsUserProfile"] = true
        ctx.Data["Title"] = org.DisplayName()   // panics here

The route is registered in `routers/web/web.go` inside the `/{username}/-`
group, which serves users as well as organizations:

    m.Get("/repositories", org.Repositories)

`context.OrgAssignment()` only fills `ctx.Org.Organization` when the context
user is an organization, so for an individual it stays nil and the next line
dereferences it. Stack from the log:

    models/user/user.go:458
    models/organization/org.go:287      (org.DisplayName)
    routers/web/org/home.go:52
    routers/web/org/home.go:45          (Repositories)

The rest of that route group already handles individuals. `org.Projects` sits
in the same group and the same package and uses `ctx.ContextUser` with an
explicit `ctx.ContextUser.IsOrganization()` branch. Anonymous, same user:

    /solo/-/projects       200
    /solo/-/code           303
    /solo/-/packages       200
    /solo/-/heatmap        200
    /solo/-/repositories   500

### Impact

Not a crash, and I would rather say so than oversell it. The panic is recovered
by `renderPanicErrorPage`, the process stays up, and the client gets a 500.

What it gives an unauthenticated caller is a log amplifier.
`renderPanicErrorPage` does `log.Error("PANIC: %v", combinedErr)` where
`combinedErr` embeds `log.Stack(2)`, unconditionally, with no gate on run mode
or stack-trace level. Measured on a stock container with `RUN_MODE = prod` and
`LEVEL = info`, repeated:

    panic request    9830, 9830, 9830 bytes of log
    normal request    152,  152 bytes

About 64x, from a single GET with no body. Sustained at 100 requests a second
that is roughly 1 MB/s, or 84 GB a day, of goroutine stack traces written to
disk by someone with no account. There is also the CPU of unwinding and
formatting each stack.

You have assigned CVEs for authenticated denial of service this year,
CVE-2026-60018 and CVE-2026-60021. This one needs no account, which is why I am
sending it, but the availability impact is disk and log volume rather than
downtime, so score it accordingly.

### A smaller thing in the same area, take it or leave it

You hide limited-visibility users from anonymous viewers and do it consistently
almost everywhere. Anonymous, against a user whose visibility is `limited`:

    /hidden                     404   correct
    /api/v1/users/hidden        404   correct
    /hidden/-/packages          404   correct
    /hidden/-/heatmap           200   discloses that the user exists
    /hidden/-/repositories      500   discloses that the user exists

A non-existent username is 404 on all five. The heatmap route returns no data
to an unauthorized viewer, only the status code differs, so this is enumeration
and nothing more. It is the same class as CVE-2026-66853, which you rated Low.
Fixing the panic fixes half of it by itself.

### Fix

Either return 404 for individuals, matching `/{username}/-/packages`, or have
`home()` handle a nil organization the way `org.Projects` already handles it.
Your call, since the route may be intended for organizations only.

### Credit

Dikshant Chandel (kewmine), Clickswave Labs Pvt Ltd.

Found during authorization research for Crossfyre (https://crossfyre.io). Being
straight about the order: I was sweeping for routes that resolve a user without
`individualPermsChecker`, after noticing that your 2026-08-29 batch fixed six
instances of that class one endpoint at a time. This route came up in that
sweep and turned out to be a panic rather than a visibility gap. So it came
from reading your advisories, not from a scanner.

---

## Also covers (added by the Gitea maintainers)

Later advisories, closed as duplicates of this one, reported the `/-/heatmap` route in the same group as a separate problem: it has no user visibility check (`individualPermsChecker` / `IsUserVisibleToViewer`), unlike its siblings `/-/projects` and `/-/code`.

- An anonymous visitor gets a 200 instead of a 404 for a private or limited user, which shows that the user exists. The heatmap data stays empty for anonymous visitors.
- A signed-in restricted user gets the contribution heatmap of a limited-visibility user, which they are not allowed to see. The API route `/api/v1/users/{username}/heatmap` already enforces this, but the web route does not.

The fix should therefore gate `/-/heatmap` with the user visibility check, in addition to returning 404 on `/-/repositories` for users who are not organizations.
advisories.summary: Unauthenticated nil-pointer panic on /{username}/-/repositories for individual users

### Summary
Any user which can edit the external issue tracker settings of a repo can crash the Gitea instance.

### Details
I accidentally released this vulnerability publicly before realizing the impact: https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/issues/39351

I already wrote a mail to the Gitea Security Team and would suggest to delete the Issue.

### What I expected
Both `123456:` and `TEST-123456` should be a link to the same external issue tracker.

advisories.description:
### Summary

Mallory is an authenticated, non-site-admin user who legitimately has repository-admin access to Alice's repository. When `IMPORT_LOCAL_PATHS = true` and Alice has permission to import local paths, Mallory can use the push-mirror API to select an absolute `file://` path on the Gitea host. The API checks Alice's local-import capability instead of Mallory's, accepts the mirror, and later runs `git push --mirror` into Mallory's selected local Git repository. This does not steal Alice's session or bypass the repository-admin requirement; it crosses the separate site-level boundary that is supposed to reserve local-filesystem imports for site administrators or specifically authorized users.

The narrow demonstrated impact is an integrity violation: a non-site-admin repository collaborator caused attacker-influenced refs and repository content to be written into a local bare Git repository that the Gitea operating-system account could write. The response behavior also revealed whether a candidate local path passed directory validation, but no arbitrary file read, operating-system command execution, or service-wide denial of service was demonstrated.

I inspected the exact source at current `main` commit `25984bef0f` (identified by the tree as `v1.28.0-dev`), the preserved HTTP end-to-end run record, and the relevant release snapshots. I did not rerun the HTTP exploit against that exact current-main binary; instead, I confirmed that its source-to-sink path is unchanged. The earliest stable release I verified with the vulnerable API call is v1.18.0. I checked 69 stable tag snapshots from v1.18.0 through v1.27.3, including the currently supported v1.27 line, and each passes the repository owner to the local-path check. No fixed release was present as of the assessed current-main snapshot.

Suggested severity: **High**, CVSS 3.1 **7.1** (`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N`). The configuration and permission prerequisites limit deployment reachability, while the demonstrated write crosses from a remote repository collaborator to a local Git repository outside the repository's normal authorization boundary.

### Details

This finding needs two distinct permissions to remain separate:

- Mallory is a normal authenticated user and an admin collaborator on `alice/project`. Repository-admin access allows her to manage that repository's push mirrors.
- Alice owns `alice/project` and is a site administrator, or has the per-user `AllowImportLocal` capability.
- The instance has the opt-in setting `[security] IMPORT_LOCAL_PATHS = true`. The shipped example configuration sets this to `false`, so this is not reachable under the default value.
- Push mirrors are enabled, and an explicitly provisioned local bare repository exists at an absolute path writable by the Gitea process.

Repository-admin access is intentionally enough to reach the API. In `routers/api/v1/api.go`, `reqAdmin` accepts an owner, a collaborator with repository-admin permission, or a site administrator:

```go
// reqAdmin user should be an owner or a collaborator with admin write of a repository, or site admin
func reqAdmin() func(ctx *context.APIContext) {
	return func(ctx *context.APIContext) {
		if !ctx.IsUserRepoAdmin() && !ctx.IsUserSiteAdmin() {
			ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, "user should be an owner or a collaborator with admin write of a repository")
			return
		}
	}
}
```

That permission should allow Mallory to configure ordinary network push mirrors for `alice/project`. It should not confer Alice's separate permission to address the server's local filesystem. `models/user/user.go` makes this capability site-admin or per-user scoped:

```go
func (u *User) CanImportLocal() bool {
	if !setting.ImportLocalPaths || u == nil {
		return false
	}
	return u.IsAdmin || u.AllowImportLocal
}
```

The tested topology used Alice as the privileged repository owner and Mallory as a non-site-admin admin collaborator. A second repository owned by Mallory was the negative control. The same Mallory credential and same local target were used for both requests.

#### Technical details

Mallory controls `remote_address` in `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/push_mirrors`. The repository routing middleware resolves `{owner}` and stores that user in `ctx.ContextUser`; it keeps the authenticated caller separately in `ctx.Doer`:

```go
ctx.Repo.Owner = owner
ctx.ContextUser = owner
```

In current `main`, `routers/api/v1/repo/mirror.go`, `CreatePushMirror` parses Mallory's supplied address and passes `ctx.ContextUser` to the migration URL policy:

```go
address, err := git.ParseRemoteAddr(mirrorOption.RemoteAddress, mirrorOption.RemoteUsername, mirrorOption.RemotePassword)
if err == nil {
	err = migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed(address, ctx.ContextUser)
}
```

For `POST /repos/alice/project/push_mirrors`, `ctx.ContextUser` is Alice even though the request is authenticated as Mallory. `services/migrations/migrate.go`, `IsMigrateURLAllowed`, then authorizes a local path using the supplied user's capability:

```go
if u.Scheme == "file" || u.Scheme == "" {
	if !doer.CanImportLocal() {
		return &git.ErrInvalidCloneAddr{Host: "<LOCAL_FILESYSTEM>", IsPermissionDenied: true, LocalPath: true}
	}
	isAbs := filepath.IsAbs(u.Host + u.Path)
	// ...existing-directory checks...
	return nil
}
```

Because the supplied user is Alice, her site-admin or `AllowImportLocal` status approves Mallory's request. The same feature's web handler in `routers/web/repo/setting/setting.go` and the repository migration API in `routers/api/v1/repo/migrate.go` both call `IsMigrateURLAllowed(..., ctx.Doer)`, showing that the effective caller is the intended principal.

After creation, the address is stored as a push-mirror remote. A sync request reaches `services/mirror/mirror_push.go`, which resolves that remote and invokes Git with `Mirror: true`:

```go
if err := git.PushToExternal(ctx, storageRepo, git.PushOptions{
	Remote:  m.RemoteName,
	Force:   true,
	Mirror:  true,
	Timeout: timeout,
	Env:     envs,
}); err != nil {
	// ...
}
```

The preserved disposable-instance run used a non-site-admin user named `mcollab` in the role described here as Mallory. With the same local bare-repository target, creating a mirror on Mallory's own repository returned `401 Permission denied`. Creating it on a site-admin-owned repository where Mallory was an admin collaborator returned `200`, and `POST .../push_mirrors-sync` returned `200`. Inspection of the target bare repository showed a new `refs/heads/main`, and `proof.txt` at that ref contained `MIRROR-WRITE-PROOF`. The report package's `poc/observed-run.md` preserves this result with the author-machine target path normalized.

Release-history inspection attributes the API endpoint to commit `0e61a74e5a` ("Add new API endpoints for push mirrors management"). v1.17.3 does not contain this vulnerable push-mirror API call; v1.18.0 does. Every inspected stable tag from v1.18.0 through v1.27.3 contains `IsMigrateURLAllowed(address, ctx.ContextUser)`. No fix was found in the assessed `main` source.

#### Suggested remediation

Evaluate the local-path policy against the authenticated caller. The source-compatible fix in `routers/api/v1/repo/mirror.go` is one principal substitution:

```diff
 address, err := git.ParseRemoteAddr(mirrorOption.RemoteAddress, mirrorOption.RemoteUsername, mirrorOption.RemotePassword)
 if err == nil {
-	err = migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed(address, ctx.ContextUser)
+	err = migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed(address, ctx.Doer)
 }
```

This matches the web push-mirror handler and migration API. It preserves repository-admin authorization for managing an ordinary mirror while requiring Mallory herself to hold the extra local-import capability before a `file://` address is accepted.

Add an API regression test with two users and the same safe temporary bare repository:

1. Alice has `AllowImportLocal` (or site-admin status); Mallory does not.
2. Mallory is an admin collaborator on Alice's repository.
3. Mallory's `file://` push-mirror creation on Alice's repository is rejected.
4. Alice's own equivalent request succeeds, proving that the feature remains available to an authorized caller.
5. An ordinary network mirror remains available to a repository admin under the normal outbound-host policy.
6. Repeat with an organization-owned repository to ensure no owner or organization principal is substituted for `ctx.Doer`.

As defense in depth, retain the caller identity or an authorization decision with the mirror record and re-check local-path authorization when editing or synchronizing a local push mirror. That would constrain stale configurations if an operator later revokes the capability. This is broader hardening; changing the creation-time principal is the direct fix for the demonstrated bug.

### Impact

The verified primitive is a wrong-principal authorization decision followed by a local Git write. Mallory must already be an admin collaborator on an Alice-owned repository, but she does not need site-admin status or her own `AllowImportLocal` capability. Alice must possess that local-import capability, the global opt-in must be enabled, and the chosen absolute path must be an existing directory accessible to the Gitea process.

The positive and negative controls isolate the principal confusion:

- Negative control: Mallory asked to mirror her own repository to the safe local target. Because `ctx.ContextUser` was Mallory and she lacked the capability, Gitea returned `401 Permission denied`.
- Positive attack: Mallory made the otherwise equivalent request against Alice's repository, on which she had repository-admin access. Because `ctx.ContextUser` became privileged Alice, Gitea returned `200` and later pushed refs to the target.
- Sink confirmation: inspecting the target with Git showed the source repository's `main` ref and the known proof content. This rules out a response-only authorization discrepancy: the local Git operation actually happened.

The demonstrated integrity boundary is narrower than arbitrary filesystem write. Git writes repository objects and refs to a valid target repository using the Gitea process's operating-system permissions. A target belonging to another service, a backup, or another tenant could make the practical impact greater, but those deployments were not tested. The test did not establish arbitrary non-Git file overwrite, hook execution, code execution, or reliable service outage.

The different validation outcomes can also be used as a limited existing-directory oracle when Alice's capability is borrowed, because absolute existing directories proceed beyond the local-path policy while invalid paths take a different error branch. The preserved run's security impact, however, rests on the confirmed Git write rather than this weaker side channel.

This issue is aligned with Gitea's attacker model because Mallory is an ordinary remote authenticated user, not a trusted instance operator. Enabling local imports is an operator choice, but the code expressly assigns that capability to particular users; the vulnerability lets an unauthorized collaborator inherit it from a repository owner.

#### Closing assessment

With the non-default `IMPORT_LOCAL_PATHS = true` setting, a non-site-admin admin collaborator can borrow a privileged repository owner's local-import capability through the push-mirror API. The vulnerable call is present in every inspected stable release from v1.18.0 through v1.27.3 and in assessed current `main` commit `25984bef0f`; no fixed release was verified. A disposable HTTP run demonstrated the distinguishing `401`/`200` behavior and confirmed that the subsequent sync wrote Git refs and controlled content to a local bare repository. The report does not claim arbitrary file overwrite or code execution. Submit this root cause as one private GitHub Security Advisory, after independent reproduction and a human rewrite as required by Gitea's reporting policy.

**CVSS v3.1:** 7.1 (`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N`)

**Weaknesses:** CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization

**AI assistance disclosure:** AI-assisted tools provided by OpenSec were used for source analysis, release-history review, PoC development and execution, and report drafting
advisories.summary: Push-mirror API checks local-path permission on the repository owner instead of the caller

advisories.description:
### Summary

Mallory, a registered user who can open a pull request from a fork, can place attacker-controlled `pull_request` workflow content into an approval-pending run and give that workflow a shared run-level `concurrency` group. A later run in that group cancels the first blocked job, leaving the run terminal and `NeedApproval=true`. When Alice, a maintainer with Actions write permission, later uses the ordinary run approval or “Approve all checks” control, Gitea passes the already-cancelled job through its concurrency preparer, changes it back to `Waiting`, and makes it claimable by a matching runner. Mallory does not steal Alice's session and cannot invoke the approval route herself; Alice's later approval action is required.

I reproduced the `Cancelled -> Waiting -> runner claim` state transition in a focused Go test against upstream `main` commit `25984bef0f` (2026-09-14). The test passed through the real `PrepareToStartRunWithConcurrency`, `ApproveRuns`, and `CreateTaskForRunner` functions. The web/API entry points and their permission checks were source-reviewed, but I did not execute this as a full browser-to-runner HTTP test. The proposed CVSS v3.1 score is **9.0 Critical** (`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`) for deployments where Actions is enabled and a matching self-hosted runner processes the repository's jobs.

The earliest release source I verified with the unsafe approval/concurrency combination is v1.26.0. The same behavior is present in inspected v1.26.x and v1.27.0–v1.27.3 snapshots and in the assessed `main` commit; no fixed release was identified. Only v1.27.x and `main` are currently in Gitea's supported security scope.

### Details

Alice owns or maintains `alice/project` and has write permission to its Actions unit. Actions are enabled, the repository accepts fork pull requests, and an Actions runner matching Mallory's `runs-on` label is available. Mallory has no write permission to `alice/project`, has no previously merged pull request there, and can only contribute through a fork. Those facts make her fork-PR run carry both `IsForkPullRequest=true` and `NeedApproval=true`.

The expected invariant is simple: only a non-terminal job that is currently blocked on approval may be released by approval. A `Cancelled` job is terminal. If Alice wants to execute it after cancellation, Gitea should require an explicit rerun operation that creates or selects a new attempt; an approval operation must not rewrite the terminal job.

Gitea exposes three relevant maintainer-only entry points:

- `POST /{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run}/approve` in `routers/web/web.go`, guarded by Actions-write permission;
- `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run}/approve` in `routers/api/v1/api.go`, guarded by an authenticated token and Actions-write permission; and
- `POST /{owner}/{repo}/actions/approve-all-checks?commit_id=...`, also guarded by Actions-write permission.

The problem is not missing authorization on these routes. It is that the authorized approval operation applies to a terminal state that approval must not revive.

#### Technical details

For a fork PR from an untrusted contributor, `ifNeedApprovalWith` in `services/actions/notifier_helper.go` correctly requires approval. This existing control was present in the assessed source and was not bypassed during run creation.

Run-level concurrency is nevertheless evaluated while the run is approval-pending. `CancelPreviousJobsByRunConcurrency` in `models/actions/run.go` deliberately includes both `Waiting` and `Blocked` jobs in the set cancelled by a later attempt:

```go
statusFindOption := []Status{StatusWaiting, StatusBlocked}
if attempt.ConcurrencyCancel {
	statusFindOption = append(statusFindOption, StatusRunning)
	statusFindOption = append(statusFindOption, StatusCancelling)
}
```

The focused test creates Mallory's first fork-PR run with a `Blocked` job and `NeedApproval=true`, then prepares a second run attempt in the same workflow-level group. The real cancellation path changes the first job to `Cancelled`; refreshing its parent also makes the run terminal while leaving `NeedApproval=true`.

The run page in `routers/web/repo/actions/view.go` computes `CanApprove` from the approval flag and permission but does not exclude a done attempt:

```go
resp.State.Run.CanApprove = isLatestAttempt && run.NeedApproval && ctx.Repo.Permission.CanWrite(unit.TypeActions)
```

Likewise, `ApproveAllChecks` selects every run recovered from the commit statuses for which `NeedApproval` remains true, without an `IsDone()` check:

```go
for _, run := range runs {
	if run.NeedApproval {
		runIDs = append(runIDs, run.ID)
	}
}
```

The decisive fault is in `ApproveRuns` in `services/actions/approve.go`. The function verifies `NeedApproval`, clears that flag, then iterates every latest-attempt job. It records whether a job was blocked for max-parallel accounting, but that Boolean does not guard the call to the concurrency preparer:

```go
if !run.NeedApproval {
	continue
}
run.NeedApproval = false
// ...
for _, job := range jobs {
	if len(job.Needs) > 0 {
		continue
	}
	isUnblocking := job.Status == actions_model.StatusBlocked
	// ...
	job.Status, jobsToCancel, err = PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency(ctx, job)
```

`PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency` in `services/actions/clear_tasks.go` has no terminal-state precondition. For a job with no job-level concurrency conflict, it returns `StatusWaiting` regardless of the input status:

```go
return util.Iif(shouldBlock, actions_model.StatusBlocked, actions_model.StatusWaiting), jobs, nil
```

`ApproveRuns` then persists `Waiting` without an optimistic condition requiring the database row still to be `Blocked`. `CreateTaskForRunner` in `models/actions/task.go` selects jobs with `task_id=0` and `status=Waiting`, so a matching runner can claim the resurrected job.

The released GHSA-v2w8-m4gr-qj65 / CVE-2026-66877 is closely related but not the same trigger or missing check. Its published title describes a fork-PR `NeedApproval` bypass through **job-level concurrency cancellation**. The v1.27.3 fix prevents the job emitter from advancing any run while `run.NeedApproval` remains true. This finding uses **workflow-level run concurrency** to produce a terminal `Cancelled` run, followed by Alice's later approval; the missing check is in `ApproveRuns`, which fails to restrict approval to a non-terminal run and `Blocked` jobs. It is therefore a missed sibling/incomplete coverage of the same security boundary, not a re-demonstration of the fixed job-emitter path.

Source history ties the unsafe transition to the Actions concurrency implementation included in v1.26.0. In v1.25.5's inspected approval code, approval only changed a job when `job.Status.IsBlocked()`; v1.26.0 instead called `PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency` for every job. Inspected v1.27.0–v1.27.3 snapshots retain that behavior, and the Actions-run-attempt refactor moved it into `services/actions/approve.go` without adding a terminal-state guard.

#### Suggested remediation

Approval should reject a terminal run or terminal latest attempt before clearing `NeedApproval`. Within the transaction, it should process only jobs whose current status is exactly `StatusBlocked`. The update should carry an optimistic database predicate such as `status = StatusBlocked`, so a concurrent cancellation cannot be overwritten between the check and write. `PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency` should never be called for `Cancelled`, `Success`, `Failure`, or `Skipped` jobs.

A source-compatible shape is:

```go
if !run.NeedApproval || run.Status.IsDone() {
	continue
}
// ...
for _, job := range jobs {
	if job.Status != actions_model.StatusBlocked || len(job.Needs) > 0 {
		continue
	}
	job.Status, jobsToCancel, err = PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency(ctx, job)
	// ...
	n, err := actions_model.UpdateRunJob(ctx, job,
		builder.Eq{"status": actions_model.StatusBlocked}, "status")
}
```

The exact fix should also decide whether approval of a terminal run returns a conflict/error or a successful no-op, and keep the web UI, batch endpoint, and API consistent. Hide approval controls for done attempts and filter done runs in `ApproveAllChecks`, but do not rely on UI filtering as the security control.

Regression tests should cover: ordinary `Blocked -> Waiting` approval; `Cancelled + NeedApproval` remaining cancelled; runner claim failing for that cancelled job; a cancellation racing with approval; workflow-level and job-level concurrency variants; the run-specific web/API routes; and the batch approval route. A fixed-target rerun of the attached test should fail at its “cancelled job was revived” assertion until the test is inverted into a regression test asserting that the job remains cancelled.

No shipped fix or fixed release was identified during this assessment.

### Impact

The narrow demonstrated primitive is a database-backed state transition: a fork-PR job that is conclusively `Cancelled` and whose run is done becomes `Waiting` after `ApproveRuns`, and `CreateTaskForRunner` returns a task whose `JobID` is that resurrected job. Before approval, the test asserts the job is `Cancelled`, the run is done, and `NeedApproval` is still true; these are the negative controls that rule out an ordinary still-blocked approval flow. After approval, it asserts `Waiting`, zero prior task ID, a successful runner claim, and the exact job ID; these observations rule out merely clearing a display flag without reaching the scheduler.

Mallory can supply the fork PR, workflow YAML, run-level concurrency group, steps, and matching `runs-on` labels. Alice must separately perform a legitimate approval action after the cancellation. The web and API routes correctly require Alice's Actions-write authority, so this is a confused state transition induced through a legitimate maintainer action, not direct low-privilege access to an approval endpoint.

When the claimed task executes on a self-hosted runner, Mallory's workflow steps run with the runner process's operating-system and network access. That can affect confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the runner host and resources reachable from it. Gitea preserves `IsForkPullRequest`, so repository and organization secrets intended to be withheld from fork PRs remain withheld; this report does not claim direct Gitea secret disclosure. Hosted or strongly isolated disposable runners reduce the durable host impact.

Constraints are material: Actions and fork-PR workflows must be enabled; the workflow must obtain a `Cancelled + NeedApproval` state, such as through a later run in the same run-level concurrency group; Alice must later approve the affected run or an approval batch containing it; and a runner matching the labels must poll for work. The focused test controls this sequence but does not measure how often maintainers approve a visibly cancelled run, nor does it prove the complete `ApproveAllChecks` status-recovery path in a live UI.

#### Closing assessment

On the assessed `main` commit and in inspected supported v1.27 release snapshots, a fork-PR run may be cancelled while still marked `NeedApproval`. A later maintainer approval passes its terminal job through `PrepareToStartJobWithConcurrency`, persists `Waiting`, and exposes the attacker-controlled job to a matching runner. The state transition and runner claim were reproduced in a focused current-source test; the maintainer routes were source-traced rather than exercised end to end. The vulnerability requires Actions, a matching runner, a shared run-level concurrency state, and a later legitimate approval action. It is a distinct missed sibling of GHSA-v2w8-m4gr-qj65 because the published fix blocks a job-emitter path, whereas this report requires a terminal-state guard in `ApproveRuns`.

**CVSS v3.1:** 9.0 (`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`)

**Weaknesses:** CWE-841: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow

**AI assistance disclosure:** AI-assisted tools provided by OpenSec were used for source analysis, release-history review, PoC development and execution, and report drafting

advisories.description:
### Summary
When a user sets their profile visibility to private, any other authenticated user can retrieve their full name, location, website and description by sending a POST /{username} request with an empty or unknown 

### Details
The root cause is that the visibility check in [routers/web/user/profile.go:54-59](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.3/routers/web/user/profile.go#L54-L59) is only performed for normal profile GET requests.

The POST route in [routers/web/web.go:911](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.3/routers/web/web.go#L911) only requires the requester to be signed in. `ActionUserFollow` in [routers/web/user/profile.go](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.3/routers/web/user/profile.go#L327-L332) does not check whether the target user is visible. An empty or unknown action is accepted because the switch has no default case, after which the private profile header is rendered and returned. 

### Impact
This vulnerability allows any authenticated user to retrieve personal information from unrelated users whose profiles are configured as private.
advisories.summary: Private profile information leaks on POST request

advisories.description:
### Summary

The fix for GHSA-v2w8-m4gr-qj65 added a NeedApproval check to the job-level concurrency path but missed the run-level one. When a fork PR is opened, InsertRun cancels older runs in the same concurrency group without checking if the new run still needs approval. This means an unapproved fork PR can kill any trusted run that shares the group, just by being opened.

### Details

notifier_helper.go correctly marks the fork PR run as needing approval before inserting it, but InsertRun never looks at that flag. The approval guard from the GHSA-v2w8-m4gr-qj65 fix only exists in job_emitter.go (checkRunConcurrency), which handles the wake/advance path. The insert-time path goes through clear_tasks.go (CancelPreviousJobsByRunConcurrency) and only matches on repo ID, concurrency group, and status. Since a fork PR run is inserted under the base repo's ID, it shares the group namespace with trusted runs and cancels them on insert.

Confirmed on Gitea 1.27.3 with act_runner 0.6.1. A deployment workflow with concurrency: { group: deploy-prod, cancel-in-progress: true } was cancelled mid-step by an unapproved fork PR. The runner was left with a migration applied but never health-checked, and a binary deployed but never verified.

### Impact

Any user who can fork a public repo and open a PR can cancel trusted CI runs at will, without approval and without running any code. On self-hosted runners, this leaves partial deployment state behind. The attack is repeatable with new PRs.
advisories.summary: Unapproved fork PR cancels trusted in-progress runs via run-level concurrency

advisories.description:
### Summary

The fork pull request approval gate decides on the **event actor** rather than the **pull request
author**. `ifNeedApprovalWith` (`services/actions/notifier_helper.go:492`, decision body at
`:499-519`) is passed `input.Doer`, bound at `:394`. For `pull_request` sub-events a maintainer fires
during ordinary triage — adding a label is the one I proved — the actor is the maintainer, the actor
passes `canWriteActions`, and the run is created with `NeedApproval=false` and dispatched to a runner
