advisories.summary: Remote Code Execution via unescaped markup `Context` into external renderer argv

cwes.name: Operation on a Resource after Expiration or Release

advisories.summary: Incorrect Authorization in Repository Transfer Allows Persistent Unauthorized Read Access

advisories.description:
### Summary

An authenticated repository collaborator with Admin access can escalate their effective permission to Owner by submitting `mode=4` to the collaboration access-mode endpoint.

After the escalation, the collaborator can perform Owner-only operations, including transferring the repository to their own account.

Confirmed on Gitea 1.27.1.

### Details

The web handler passes the submitted `uid` and `mode` directly to `ChangeCollaborationAccessMode`:

https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.1/routers/web/repo/setting/collaboration.go#L111-L116

The model accepts permission values up to and including `AccessModeOwner`:

https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.1/models/repo/collaboration.go#L103-L132

The relevant validation is:

```go
if mode <= perm.AccessModeNone || mode > perm.AccessModeOwner {
    return nil
}
```

Because only values greater than `AccessModeOwner` are rejected, `mode=4` is accepted and written to both `collaboration.mode` and the effective `access.mode`.

Owner checks rely on this effective access mode:

[https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.1/models/perm/access/repo_permission.go#L35-L38](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/blob/v1.27.1/models/perm/access/repo_permission.go#L35-L38)

### Impact

This is an authenticated privilege-escalation vulnerability.

Any user who has been granted Admin collaborator access to a repository can obtain effective Owner permissions and perform operations that should be restricted to the repository owner. The demonstrated impact is takeover of a private repository by transferring it to the attacker's account.

The issue also affects repositories owned by regular user accounts and is not limited to organization-owned repositories.
advisories.summary: Admin repository collaborator can self-escalate to Owner and transfer the repository

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers or Frames

advisories.description:
`modules/markup/jupyter/jupyter.go` sets `SanitizerDisabled: true` but leaves
`DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` at their zero values. It is the only
renderer in the tree that turns the sanitizer off while still rendering into the
main document. Within that unsanitized output it interpolates
`notebook.metadata.language_info.name` — a value read directly from the file —
into a literal `class` attribute without routing it through
`RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs`.

HTML-escaping prevents closing the attribute, but whitespace is untouched, so
the notebook can choose its own list of CSS classes on a page where nothing
filters them. Combined with Fomantic's `.ui.dimmer` and Gitea's `!important`
Tailwind layer, a repository file can replace the entire viewport of a
repository page and intercept clicks on it.

Script execution was not reached. The reason to fix this is not the overlay:
it is that the class attribute is the one place on this path where a security
control was skipped, and there is no sanitizer, no iframe sandbox and no CSP
behind it.

## Why this is a boundary failure rather than a cosmetic bug

Gitea has a deliberate mechanism to stop rendered content from choosing CSS
classes. `RenderInternal.ProtectSafeAttrs` rewrites `class="X"` into
`data-attr-class="<per-render-nonce>:X"`; the sanitizer allows `data-attr-class`;
and `finalProcessor.Close` converts it back only when the nonce matches. Content
cannot forge the nonce, so only the renderer's own trusted code can emit a class.
`orgmode.go` uses this correctly:

```go
_ = ctx.RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs(sb, `<pre><code class="chroma language-%s">`, ...)
```

The intent is also written down inside the affected file itself, in the
`text/html` MIME handler:

```go
// To future developers:  don't allow custom CSS classes or attributes,
// because ".link-action" or "data-fetch-xxx" can send POST requests and lead to XSS.
```

That rule is enforced for MIME output and missed for the language field.

## Details

**1. The sanitizer is disabled and the output is not confined.**

```go
func (renderer) GetExternalRendererOptions() markup.ExternalRendererOptions {
  return markup.ExternalRendererOptions{
    SanitizerDisabled: true,
  }
}
```

`DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` are left unset. In `modules/markup/render.go`
that removes `SanitizeReader` from the pipeline, and the bytes land inside
`<div class="file-view markup jupyter-render">` on the ordinary repository page.

By contrast the `openapi-swagger`, `viewer-3d` and `asciicast` renderers also
disable the sanitizer, but set `DisplayInIframe: true` and
`ContentSandbox: setting.MarkupRenderDefaultSandbox`, so their output is confined
to an iframe with no `allow-same-origin`.

**2. Untrusted input reaches a literal `class` attribute.**

The `language` value comes from `notebook.metadata.language_info.name`, falling
back to `metadata.kernelspec.language`, and is interpolated into a
`class="chroma language-…"` attribute. `htmlutil.WriteFormat` applies
`template.HTMLEscapeString`, which handles `< > & ' "` and leaves whitespace
alone. No input yields a raw `"`, so no new attribute can be created — but
spaces pass through, which is enough to append arbitrary additional CSS classes.

**3. `/render/` serves the same content with no CSP.**

The `/render/` route adds a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox …` header only when
the renderer sets `ContentSandbox`, a field the Jupyter renderer never sets. The
result is a top-level, same-origin, navigable `text/html` document built from
repository content, with the sanitizer off and no restrictions, reachable
anonymously on public repositories. Repository authorization on the route itself
is sound (private repositories return 404 to unauthorized users).

**4. The notebook selects which frontend renderer processes it.**

Because the class is built as `language-%s` from the file, a notebook can declare
`"language_info": {"name": "mermaid"}` (or `math`) and hand its cell source to
mermaid.js / KaTeX. Those frontend paths assign markup via `innerHTML` in the
parent document before moving it into a non-sandboxed iframe. Today mermaid's
`securityLevel: 'strict'` and KaTeX's `trust: false` hold, so script execution
was not achieved — but this is the same unsanitized, no-CSP surface, reached from
a file type where nothing signals that a diagram will be drawn.

## Impact

Anyone with write access to a repository can make its pages display arbitrary
full-screen content on the Gitea origin, with the real hostname and certificate,
and make the underlying page unusable. Pushed to a shared repository, it affects
every colleague who opens that repository, with no link sent and no unusual
action taken — making fake session-expiry notices, credential-rotation
instructions or outage banners credible because the instance itself serves them.

Two bounds are worth stating explicitly:

- **It does not cross a permission boundary.** The attacker needs write access to
  the repository holding the notebook; read-only access is not enough. Existing
  repository permissions are respected.
- **The overlay is text.** The cell body passes through chroma, so there is no
  input, button or link. A credential prompt must end in "go to this other host",
  which the victim types by hand.

## Remediation

Upgrade to a fixed release. Until then, avoid rendering or serving untrusted
`.ipynb` files (for example by disabling the Jupyter renderer on instances that
accept notebooks from untrusted contributors).

## Reporter

Toprak Yagcioglu. Found and reproduced against a local throwaway
`gitea/gitea:1.27.1` container; nothing was tested against any third-party or
production instance. Happy to supply a reproduction and to verify a candidate
patch.
advisories.summary: Jupyter notebook renderer emits attacker-controlled CSS classes into unsanitized, unsandboxed output

cwes.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

advisories.description:
### Summary
When a Maven artifact is uploaded with a checksum extension (`.md5`, `.sha1`, `.sha256`, `.sha512`), the handler reads the entire request body into memory and compares it to the stored digest, then returns — before the code path that enforces the package size quota. The checksum branch therefore has neither a size quota nor any bound on how much is read into memory, although a valid checksum value is at most 128 bytes.

### Details
The body is read with `io.ReadAll` and copied again for the comparison; both allocations are sized by the client. The configured `LIMIT_SIZE_MAVEN` is not applied to this path. Reachable by any authenticated user with Maven package write access.

### Impact
Package size-quota bypass and client-controlled memory allocation for a single request (uncontrolled resource consumption). A practical outage was not demonstrated; the issue should be read as an unbounded allocation and a quota bypass.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39028, #39031).

### Workarounds
Limit request body size at the reverse proxy. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Package size quota bypass and unbounded memory read in the Maven checksum upload path

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

advisories.description:
### Summary
Gitea implements repository visibility with several SQL predicates that are meant to be equivalent. One of them, used by the accessible-repository condition, treats repositories owned by hidden users differently from the others. As a result, some repository-listing endpoints return repositories owned by hidden users even though those repositories are unreachable through their direct routes, which still return `404`.

### Details
The authenticated repository-search API is the broadest affected surface; the forks listing is also affected for anonymous users, and watched repositories for users already subscribed.

### Impact
Any authenticated user can enumerate repositories owned by hidden users through repository search; anonymous users can do so through the forks listing. Metadata disclosure only.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39009, #39012).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Repository listing exposes repositories owned by hidden users due to inconsistent visibility predicate

advisories.description:
### Summary
The `gitignores` field of the repository-creation form and API option struct has no maximum-length constraint. During repository initialization the field is split on commas and each name triggers a template read whose result is buffered in memory before `.gitignore` is written. A large attacker-controlled value therefore produces a proportional number of template reads and in-memory buffering.

### Details
Reachable through `POST /repo/create` and `POST /api/v1/user/repos` (and the organization equivalent) when auto-init is enabled.

### Impact
Uncontrolled resource consumption during repository creation, proportional to the submitted field length. Availability only.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39027, #39040).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Unbounded gitignores repository-creation field enables linear template-read amplification

advisories.description:
# Title: Installer Re-run Against an Already-Populated Database Grants an Authenticated Session for an Existing Admin Account Without Password Verification

**Affected component:** `routers/install/install.go`, `models/db/install/db.go`
**Affected version tested:** Gitea v1.27.1 (Docker image `gitea/gitea:1.27.1`)
**Vulnerability class:** CWE-287 (Improper Authentication), CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical Function)
**Suggested severity:** High (CVSS 3.1 vector estimate below)

---

## 1. Summary

When Gitea's web installer (`/install`) is reachable against a database that **already contains user accounts** (i.e. an installed/previously-used instance whose `INSTALL_LOCK` has been reset to `false`), submitting the install form with an `Administrator Username` that matches an **existing** user causes the installer to:

1. Silently fall back to loading the existing user record (`GetUserByName`) after `CreateUser` fails with `ErrUserAlreadyExist`, without verifying the password supplied in the install form against that user's stored credentials.
2. Immediately issue a valid "remember me" auth token and a fully authenticated web session (`uid`/`uname`) for that existing user — including full `IsAdmin` privileges if the existing user is an admin.
3. Allow the now-authenticated attacker to reach `/-/admin/users/{id}/edit` and set a **new password of their choosing** for that account, with no requirement to supply the account's original (old) password.

The net effect is that an attacker who can reach the install page of a Gitea instance whose database still holds prior user data, and who can guess or otherwise learn a valid username (commonly `admin` or similar, or discoverable via public profile pages / commit authorship on the same instance), can take over that account — including a first-created admin account — **without ever knowing its original password.**

A secondary contributing issue is that the "reinstall confirmation" safeguard (3 checkboxes normally required when Gitea detects a pre-existing installation) does **not** trigger in a common real-world case: production databases with exactly one existing user, because the "has post-installation users" heuristic uses a threshold of 2 (see §3.2).

---

## 2. Affected Code

### 2.1 `routers/install/install.go` — `checkDatabase()`

```go
hasPostInstallationUser, err := db_install.HasPostInstallationUsers(ctx)
...
dbMigrationVersion, err := db_install.GetMigrationVersion(ctx)
...
if hasPostInstallationUser && dbMigrationVersion > 0 {
    log.Error("The database is likely to have been used by Gitea before, database migration version=%d", dbMigrationVersion)
    confirmed := form.ReinstallConfirmFirst && form.ReinstallConfirmSecond && form.ReinstallConfirmThird
    if !confirmed {
        ctx.Data["Err_DbInstalledBefore"] = true
        ctx.RenderWithErrDeprecated(ctx.Tr("install.reinstall_error"), tplInstall, form)
        return false
    }
    log.Info("User confirmed re-installation of Gitea into a pre-existing database")
}
```

### 2.2 `models/db/install/db.go` — `HasPostInstallationUsers()`

```go
// if there are 2 or more users in database, we consider there are users created after installation
threshold := 2
if !setting.IsProd {
    threshold = 1
}
res, err := x.Table("user").Cols("id").Limit(threshold).Query()
...
return len(res) >= threshold, nil
```

### 2.3 `routers/install/install.go` — `SubmitInstall()` (admin account creation)

```go
if len(form.AdminName) > 0 {
    u := &user_model.User{
        Name:    form.AdminName,
        Email:   form.AdminEmail,
        Passwd:  form.AdminPasswd,
        IsAdmin: true,
    }
    ...
    if err = user_model.CreateUser(ctx, u, &user_model.Meta{}, overwriteDefault); err != nil {
        if !user_model.IsErrUserAlreadyExist(err) {
            setting.InstallLock = false
            ...
            return
        }
        log.Info("Admin account already exist")
        u, _ = user_model.GetUserByName(ctx, u.Name)   // <-- existing user adopted, no password check
    }

    nt, token, err := auth_service.CreateAuthTokenForUserID(ctx, u.ID)   // <-- unconditional token issuance
    ...
    ctx.SetSiteCookie(setting.CookieRememberName, nt.ID+":"+token, setting.LogInRememberDays*timeutil.Day)

    // Auto-login for admin
    ctx.Session.Set("uid", u.ID)
    ctx.Session.Set("uname", u.Name)
    ctx.Session.Release()
}
```

### 2.4 Confirmed absence of any gating check

- `user_model.IsUsableUsername()` only validates format and checks a reserved-name list; it performs **no existence check**, so a duplicate username passes this validation unimpeded.
- `auth_service.CreateAuthTokenForUserID()` issues a token unconditionally for any `userID` passed in; it does not check `IsActive`, `ProhibitLogin`, or any account state.
- `services/auth/session.go` (`Session.Verify`) later accepts this session on all subsequent requests by simply loading the user by the `uid` stored in the session — no additional re-validation.

---

## 3. Real-World Deployability (why this is not just a "self-inflicted misconfiguration")

A likely objection is: *"`INSTALL_LOCK=false` on a database with existing data is a misconfiguration nobody should hit in practice."* In our assessment this happens more often than it should, for reasons independent of any single admin's mistake:

### 3.1 Container/orchestration state drift
Gitea's official Docker image and most Helm charts persist `INSTALL_LOCK` inside `app.ini` on a mounted volume, while `INSTALL_LOCK` can *also* be supplied as an environment variable (`GITEA__security__INSTALL_LOCK`). In practice we see three common drift scenarios:

- **Volume/PVC replacement without the config file**: an operator provisions a *new* data volume (e.g. after a storage migration, disaster-recovery restore, or a Kubernetes PVC that got recreated) but restores only the **database** (external managed Postgres/MySQL is common in production, decoupled from the app data volume) — not `app.ini`. The container starts with a fresh, empty `/data/gitea/conf`, so `INSTALL_LOCK` defaults to unset/false, while the external DB is fully populated with real user data. This is exactly the precondition reproduced in our PoC.
- **`docker-compose`/Helm values regression**: `GITEA__security__INSTALL_LOCK=false` (or omitted) being (re)applied during a redeploy, e.g. a values file used for a *staging* environment accidentally applied to a production release that shares the same database, or a CI/CD pipeline reusing a base compose file that never had the lock env var added post-launch. This exact class of misconfiguration is visible in public Gitea issue trackers (e.g. issue reports where users manually toggle `INSTALL_LOCK` via env var during troubleshooting and are surprised the installer reappears).
- **Config file corruption/loss with DB left intact**: `app.ini` lives on ephemeral or under-backed-up local storage while the DB (often externally managed) is backed up independently and durable; a node replacement, disk failure, or bad rollback can wipe the app-data volume while the DB survives untouched.

### 3.2 The reinstall-confirmation safeguard has a real, common blind spot
Even when `INSTALL_LOCK` is genuinely (mistakenly) `false` against a used database, Gitea's own designed mitigation — the 3-checkbox "this will reinstall into an existing database" confirmation — is intended to catch exactly this case. However:

`HasPostInstallationUsers()` only returns `true` once the `user` table holds **2 or more** rows. Any production Gitea instance that was bootstrapped with a single administrator account and never had a second user created (a very common footprint for small teams, personal/self-hosted instances, or CI-only Gitea deployments used purely as an internal Git host with no additional accounts) will have `hasPostInstallationUser=false` regardless of how high its `dbMigrationVersion` is. Our PoC reproduced this exactly: a database at `dbMigrationVersion=343` (i.e. very much a used, long-lived database) with a single admin user did **not** trigger the reinstall-confirmation screen at all — the installer proceeded as if this were a brand-new database.

This means the safeguard that Gitea already ships specifically to prevent "installer run against existing data" incidents is silently bypassed for what is likely the single most common real-world footprint: a small self-hosted instance with one admin account.

### 3.3 Attacker does not need privileged network position
The install page is served on the same host/port as the normal application (`/install`, `/` when `INSTALL_LOCK=false`). No additional network access, credentials, or insider position is required beyond what's needed to reach the instance's normal web UI — i.e. the same exposure surface as the login page itself. If the instance is internet-facing (a common setup for small teams/open-source projects self-hosting Gitea), the install page becomes reachable to anyone the moment the drift described in §3.1 occurs, with no additional reconnaissance beyond noticing `/install` returns the installer wizard instead of redirecting to `/user/login`.

### 3.4 Username discovery is trivial
Gitea instances routinely expose usernames through:
- Public user profile pages (`/{username}`), if `RequireSignInView` is off (a common default for open-source-friendly self-hosted instances).
- Commit author metadata on any public/internal repository.
- Organization member listings.
- The very fact that `id=1` is virtually always the first admin created during initial setup — attacker can enumerate `/-/admin/users` *after* takeover to confirm, but a plausible first guess (`admin`, project owner's known handle, etc.) is often sufficient before that.

No password guessing, credential stuffing, or brute force is required — only the **username** of an existing (ideally admin) account.

### 3.5 Composite realistic attack scenario
> A small organization self-hosts Gitea on a VPS/Kubernetes cluster with `INSTALL_LOCK` stored only in the local `app.ini` on the app-data volume, and MySQL/Postgres/SQLite as a separately-backed-up (and thus more durable) datastore. A disk/volume issue, botched migration, or redeploy from a base image/Helm chart without carrying over the previously-tuned config causes the app-data volume to be re-provisioned empty while the database is intact and reachable. The instance restarts, boots into the installer, and briefly exposes `/install`. An attacker (or automated scanner probing for the well-known `/install` wizard string) reaches it, submits `AdminName=admin` (or a username seen on a public repo commit) with a password of their choosing, and is granted an authenticated admin session — followed by a self-service password reset via `/-/admin/users/{id}/edit`, converting the temporary session into permanent account ownership.

This is not a hypothetical purely-configuration-error scenario requiring an admin to *intentionally* misconfigure a fresh production system; it is a realistic failure mode of ordinary operational events (volume/DB decoupling, redeploys, disaster recovery) combined with a safeguard (`HasPostInstallationUsers`) whose threshold silently excludes the most common small-instance footprint.

---

## 5. Impact

- **Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability:** Full compromise of the targeted account, including administrative control of the Gitea instance if the targeted account is an admin (repository access across the instance, user management, instance configuration, ability to add/remove other admins, SSH key management, webhook/CI configuration, etc.).
- **Attack complexity:** Low once the precondition (`INSTALL_LOCK=false` against a used DB) exists — a single HTTP POST plus a couple of authenticated UI actions.
- **Privileges required:** None (no valid credentials needed at any point).
- **User interaction:** None (fully attacker-driven).
- **Scope:** Can change (an attacker without any account can end up with full admin control over other users' data/repos).
**CVSS 3.1 estimate:** `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **8.1 (High)**.

The attack requires a specific deployment state outside the attacker's
control: the installer must be reachable while Gitea is connected to an
already-populated database (`INSTALL_LOCK=false`). Once that state exists,
exploitation requires no authentication or user interaction and results in
full compromise of the targeted administrator account.

We defer final scoring to the Gitea security team.
---

## 6. Suggested Remediation

We suggest addressing this at two independent layers (either would substantially reduce risk; both together close it entirely):

1. **Do not silently "adopt" an existing user on `ErrUserAlreadyExist`.** The installer should either:
   - Fail hard with a clear error ("An account with this username already exists; installer cannot proceed") and require explicit reinstall confirmation regardless of the `hasPostInstallationUser`/`dbMigrationVersion` heuristic, **or**
   - Require verification of the *existing* account's current password before granting any session for it.
   In either case, the installer must never call `CreateAuthTokenForUserID` / establish a session for a user record it did not just create in this request.

2. **Fix the reinstall-confirmation blind spot.** Change the guard in `checkDatabase()` from `hasPostInstallationUser && dbMigrationVersion > 0` to `hasPostInstallationUser || dbMigrationVersion > 0` (or lower/remove the `threshold := 2` special case, which appears intended only to tolerate the installer's own first-admin creation within the *same* install run — a distinction that could instead be made by comparing user count *before* vs. *after* the current request, rather than via a static threshold against the database's total user count).

---
advisories.summary: Installer Re-run Against an Already-Populated Database Grants an Authenticated Session for an Existing Admin Account Without Password Verification

advisories.description:
### Summary
The Gitea Actions workflow status badge endpoint does not enforce the scope of the Personal Access Token (PAT) used to authenticate the request. A token that lacks `read:repository` (for example one limited to `read:user`), or a token explicitly restricted with `public-only`, can retrieve the latest workflow run status of a private repository that the token owner can access. The same tokens are correctly rejected on the private repository's web routes, so scope enforcement is inconsistent between endpoints.

### Details
The badge handler resolves the repository and returns the latest run status without applying the API token scope check that other repository read endpoints use. The badge handler has been present since Gitea 1.22.0.

### Impact
A holder of a deliberately restricted token can determine whether a named private workflow most recently succeeded, failed, is waiting or is running, and can poll it to monitor private CI activity. No repository content is modified and no file contents are returned. CWE-863 (Incorrect Authorization).

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39044, #39058).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Gitea workflow badge bypasses API token scopes

advisories.description:
The `POST /user/openid/connect` handler did not enforce second-factor authentication. An attacker who knew a victim's password could obtain a full authenticated session by submitting that password through the OpenID connect flow instead of the normal login form, bypassing TOTP and WebAuthn checks entirely.

The same request could attach an attacker-controlled OpenID identifier to the victim's account before sign-in completed. Because the OpenID sign-in path also lacked a second-factor check, the attacker could subsequently authenticate using that identifier alone — without the victim's password or second factor. Changing the victim's password did not remove the linked identifier.

OpenID sign-in is enabled by default on instances set up through the installer.

## Affected Versions

Confirmed on **1.27.1**. All versions that expose the OpenID connect endpoint and support TOTP or WebAuthn second factors should be assumed affected until verified otherwise.

## Impact

**Who was affected:** Users on instances with OpenID sign-in enabled who had enrolled TOTP or WebAuthn as a second factor.

**What broke:** Second-factor enrollment is intended to make a leaked password survivable. The OpenID connect path removed that protection for enrolled users. Password-based login continued to enforce the second-factor challenge as expected.

**Persistent access:** The connect handler wrote the attacker's OpenID identifier to the victim's account before granting the session. Subsequent OpenID sign-ins using that identifier required neither the victim's password nor a second factor. Password rotation did not revoke this access; the linked identifier had to be removed manually from account settings.

**`TWO_FACTOR_AUTH = enforced` did not mitigate this.** The enforced setting relied on a session flag set at sign-in time. Because enrolled users were flagged as having completed second-factor setup, hijacked sessions passed the enforced check rather than being challenged again.

| Attack vector | Prerequisites | Consequence |
|---------------|---------------|-------------|
| OpenID connect with password | Victim's password; OpenID sign-in enabled | Full session without second-factor challenge |
| OpenID sign-in via linked identifier | Prior successful connect attack | Full session without password or second factor; survives password change |

On a compromised Gitea account, an attacker gained access to repositories, CI secrets, Actions configuration, and push permissions for everything the user could write to. Administrator accounts exposed the entire instance.

## Root Cause

`ConnectOpenIDPost` (`routers/web/auth/openid.go`) authenticated the user with `auth.UserSignIn`, discarded the returned authentication source (which carries the second-factor policy), linked a new OpenID identifier to the account, and called `handleSignIn` — none of which consulted TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment.

The password login handler (`SignInPost` in `routers/web/auth/auth.go`) checked `TwoFactorShouldSkip()`, TOTP enrollment, and WebAuthn registration before granting a session. Those checks were absent from the OpenID connect flow.

OpenID 2.0 identities are stored in the `user_openid` table rather than as a configurable authentication source, so there was no per-source setting that could explain the missing enforcement.
advisories.summary: 2FA bypass and persistent account takeover via OpenID identity linking

advisories.description:
### Summary
The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository.

### Details
The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status.

### Impact
Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads

advisories.description:
### Summary
In a private repository, a member with only Wiki access can use `POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup` to resolve a same-repository pull request reference and receive the pull request title and state icon, despite having no Issues or Pull Requests access.

### Details
The markup route accepts any one of Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Releases or Wiki access. The renderer's unit check for referenced issues and pull requests is applied only in the cross-repository branch, so a same-repository reference reaches title and icon rendering without a unit check. No bodies, comments or attachments are returned.

### Impact
Confidentiality. A Wiki-only member can read pull request titles and displayed state from a private repository.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39045, #39054).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Wiki-only members can read private pull request titles through markup preview

advisories.description:
When a push mirror runs, `runPushSync` reads the stored remote address and hands it straight to `git push`. Nothing checks that address against the `[migrations]` allow and block list. The address was checked once when the mirror was created and never again. Whatever the name resolves to at sync time is what the server connects to.

Two things follow from that. The host block list stops being an egress control, because a blocked host is still reached on every sync. And the server can be aimed at internal git services and made to force write into them.

Any registered user can do this. Adding a push mirror needs repository admin and every user has that on repositories they create themselves.

**The code**

`services/mirror/mirror_push.go`, inside `performPush`:

```
131:  remoteURL, err := git.ParseRemoteAddressURL(ctx, storageRepo, m.RemoteName)
159:  if err := git.PushToExternal(ctx, storageRepo, git.PushOptions{...}); err != nil {
```

Between those two lines there is no host check. `git.PushToExternal` shells out so the connection never passes through `modules/hostmatcher`. The same function also pushes the repository wiki through the same unchecked path at lines 178 to 187.

**Why the check belongs there**

Four separate things in the tree say so and none of them depends on the others.

Creating a push mirror is validated. `routers/web/repo/setting/setting.go:495` and `routers/api/v1/repo/mirror.go:359` both call `migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed`. The list already governs push mirrors by design. It is simply applied once and the attacker chooses the moment at which it runs.

The LFS half of `runPushSync` is guarded. At line 147 it builds its client with `migrations.NewMigrationHTTPTransport` whose dialer enforces the same list. When the host is blocked that branch stops with Gitea's own error, three lines above the `git push` that ignores the identical block.

```
Post ".../info/lfs/objects/batch": dial tcp 1.2.3.4:4000: migration can not call blocked HTTP servers (check your migrations.BLOCKED_DOMAINS setting) deny '1.2.3.4(1.2.3.4:4000)'
```

One sync operation. Two outbound paths. One of them enforces the policy and the other does not.

```
// Recheck that the remote address is still permitted before pushing. The address passed
// IsPushMirrorURLAllowed ...
// The remote URL passed IsPushMirrorURLAllowed but any redirection URL may not. Prohibit
// redirects ...
```

None of `recheckPushPermitted` or `IsPushMirrorURLAllowed` or `ProhibitHTTPRedirect` appears anywhere in Gitea.

Pull mirror sync does the check. `runSync` in `services/mirror/mirror_pull.go` parses the address the same way and then calls `migrations.IsMigrateURLAllowed` at lines 117 to 125, with a comment saying the host may now resolve somewhere internal or the list may have changed since. Two separate security changes put that behaviour there and each one touched only the pull file.

```
$ git show 97078b96cf --name-only --format=''
services/mirror/mirror_pull.go

$ git show f69e15afe7 --name-only --format='' | grep -i mirror
services/mirror/mirror_pull.go
tests/integration/mirror_pull_test.go
```

`97078b96cf` is #38320 which disabled HTTP redirects during pull mirror sync. `f69e15afe7` is #38406 which added the revalidation. Its 1.27 backport is `de4b8277e9` on `release/v1.27` so it will not resolve on `main`.

**Affected**

Every release since push mirroring shipped in 1.15.0 is affected, up to and
including 1.27.1, and main at a30d865b781b4611826bf44d60e44d9f6e8fdf4e. The
check has never been present on this path. Across every stable tag the string
IsMigrateURLAllowed appears zero times in services/mirror/mirror_push.go. The
only host aware call in that file today is the LFS transport at line 147.

```
$ git show v1.27.1:services/mirror/mirror_pull.go | grep -c IsMigrateURLAllowed
1
$ git show v1.27.1:services/mirror/mirror_push.go | grep -c IsMigrateURLAllowed
0
```

Confirmed against the released 1.27.1 binary and a build of `main` at that revision.

**Force write into an internal git service**

The mirror is created while its hostname resolves to a public address, which is allowed. The name is then repointed at an internal git service and the sync is triggered. Because the push is `--mirror --force` the refs already on the internal repository that are absent from the source are deleted and the source refs are written in their place.

I am not reporting the redirect behaviour as a bug. #38108 added `http.followRedirects=false`, #38320 extended it to pull mirror sync, and #38530 reverted it deliberately because it broke cloning GitLab URLs with no `.git` suffix, which is why `HandleGitCmdHTTPRedirection` is an empty function today. This script is here for two reasons only. It shows the attack needs no DNS control, which is what puts AC at Low. And `runPushSync` does not call that function either, so restoring the redirect behaviour later would still leave this path open.

**Impact**

The server connects to hosts the operator has blocked and force writes into internal git repositories, deleting refs that are already there.

Once the mirror exists this keeps happening on its own. The same code is reached by the interval scheduler and by sync on commit as well as by the manual button and the API endpoint. Nothing further is required from the attacker.

Reading is limited but not nothing. `last_error` is rendered back in the repository settings page and it discloses the internal repository ref names, its HEAD branch, and the commit id of any ref whose name also exists on the source side.

The stored mirror credentials go wherever the name now points. In the case above those credentials belong to the attacker so nothing is gained by it, but the same missing check means an operator's push mirror to a legitimate host will hand its credentials to whatever that name resolves to at sync time.

All of the above runs on stock defaults. Mirrors enabled, empty allow and block lists, `ALLOW_LOCALNETWORKS=false`.

Two limits stated plainly. Writing into an internal git service needs that service to accept unauthenticated receive pack. And `runPushSync` runs the guarded LFS branch before the git push, so if `LFS_START_SERVER` is on and the source repository holds an LFS object the sync stops in that branch before reaching the push. An attacker who authors the source repository keeps it free of LFS objects. With `LFS_START_SERVER` off the branch is skipped.

What does stop this today is `[mirror] ENABLED=false`, which halts all mirror updates, or deleting the mirror. The per host block does not.
advisories.summary: Gitea Push Mirror Host Policy Bypass Enables SSRF and Forced Writes to Internal Git Repositories

advisories.description:
### Summary
Gitea requires maintainer approval before running fork pull request workflows when the author lacks Actions write on the base repository. That gate is skipped for the `pull_request_review_comment` event (the same code path also covers review approved/rejected), because the review notifier does not attach the pull request to the notification. With no pull request attached the run is not recognized as a fork pull request and approval is not required, while the workflow definition is still loaded from the fork head and run on the base repository's runners.

### Details
The sibling review-request notifier does attach the pull request; the review notifier does not. Present since the fork pull request approval gate was introduced in Gitea 1.20.0. An actor needs to be able to fork the repository, open a fork pull request, and submit a review with a line comment; they do not need Actions write on the base repository or a runner on the fork.

### Impact
Unapproved execution of attacker-controlled workflow code on the base repository's runners. On a privileged or host runner this is code execution as the runner user, with possible access to secrets depending on event rules; on a sandboxed runner it is unauthorized CI/compute use.

### Affected versions
Gitea `>= 1.20.0, <= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018).

### Workarounds
Instances that do not run fork pull request workflows on self-hosted runners are not exposed to the code-execution impact. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Gitea Actions: fork pull request approval bypass via `pull_request_review_comment` (missing `WithPullRequest`)

advisories.description:
## Summary

Seven API endpoints under `/api/v1/users/{username}` bypass the target user's visibility setting because they're in a route group that's missing the `individualPermsChecker` middleware. A user who sets their profile to "private" is still fully exposed through these routes.

## Root cause

In `routers/api/v1/api.go`, there are two `/users/{username}` route groups. The first one (around line 1072) correctly applies `individualPermsChecker`:

```go
m.Group("/{username}", func() {
    m.Get("", reqExploreSignIn(), user.GetInfo)
    m.Get("/heatmap", user.GetUserHeatmapData)
    m.Get("/repos", ..., user.ListUserRepos)
    m.Get("/activities/feeds", user.ListUserActivityFeeds)
}, context.UserAssignmentAPI(), checkTokenPublicOnly(), individualPermsChecker)
```

The second group (around line 1091) serves the social graph, keys, and starred/watched repos but omits that middleware:

```go
m.Group("/{username}", func() {
    m.Get("/keys", user.ListPublicKeys)
    m.Get("/gpg_keys", user.ListGPGKeys)
    m.Get("/followers", user.ListFollowers)
    m.Get("/following", user.ListFollowing)
    m.Get("/following/{target}", user.CheckFollowing)
    m.Get("/starred", reqStarsEnabled(), user.GetStarredRepos)
    m.Get("/subscriptions", user.GetWatchedRepos)
}, context.UserAssignmentAPI(), checkTokenPublicOnly())
//                                                    ^ individualPermsChecker missing
```

None of the seven handler functions do their own visibility check internally either, so the gap is real.

## Affected endpoints

| Route | What leaks |
|-------|-----------|
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/followers` | Full follower list |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/following` | Full following list |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/following/{target}` | Whether user follows someone specific |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/starred` | Starred repos (interests, projects they watch) |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/subscriptions` | Watched repos (active involvement) |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/keys` | SSH public keys |
| `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/gpg_keys` | GPG keys (often contain email and real name) |

## Impact

For orgs using private visibility to protect employee identities (gov, defense, security teams), this completely defeats the privacy control via API. An attacker with any valid token can pull a private user's social graph, identify colleagues and collaborators, grab their SSH/GPG keys for cross-platform correlation, and see what projects they're involved with.

The GPG key endpoint is particularly bad since keys typically embed real names and email addresses.

## Fix

One-word fix — add `individualPermsChecker` to the second group's middleware chain:

```go
}, context.UserAssignmentAPI(), checkTokenPublicOnly(), individualPermsChecker)
```

## Related: org permission enumeration

While I was in this area I also noticed `GET /api/v1/users/{username}/orgs/{org}/permissions` (in `routers/api/v1/org/org.go`, `GetUserOrgsPermissions`) lets any authenticated user query any other user's exact role in any visible org — none, read, write, admin, or owner. There's no check that the requester should be allowed to see another user's permissions. This lets you map out who the admins and owners are across an entire Gitea instance.

## Related: private org existence leak

Two org routes are missing the `reqOrgVisible()` middleware that their siblings have:
- `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/repos` (line ~1721)
- `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}/activities/feeds` (line ~1764)

Compare with `/members`, `/public_members`, `/labels` which all have `reqOrgVisible()`. Lower severity since repo data is still filtered by per-repo perms, but it confirms existence of private orgs.

## Verification

All findings verified against main branch commit 20221e1 (2026-07-23). Source review only — no live instances were tested.

Regards,
Luke Granto
advisories.summary: API routes for user social graph, keys, and starred repos bypass private visibility check

advisories.description:
### Summary
`GET /api/v1/orgs` does not enforce the `read:organization` token scope. A token with only `read:misc` can list organization metadata through this endpoint. If the token belongs to a site administrator, the response includes organizations of all visibilities visible to that administrator, including limited and private ones. The single-organization endpoint `GET /api/v1/orgs/{org}` correctly requires `read:organization`.

### Impact
An API token without `read:organization` can list organization metadata visible to the token owner; for a site-admin token this includes private and limited organization metadata. Token scope boundary bypass, confidentiality.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39041, #39058).

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Token Scope Bypass on `GET /api/v1/orgs`

advisories.description:
### Summary
The fix for CVE-2026-58443 added a "token can access repository" check to `UpdatePullRequest` only. The shared helper `parseCompareInfo`, used by the compare-diff endpoint and by pull request creation, lacked the same check. A `public-only, read:repository` token can read commit history and diff content of a private head repository by routing the request through a public base repository.

### Details
The route-level public-only middleware validates only the base repository named in the route. The head repository resolved inside `parseCompareInfo` is checked for user permission but not against the token's scope. Two entry points reach it:

1. `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{basehead}` with `head` given as `owner/repo:branch`. The head repository does not need to be a fork of the base.
2. `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls` with the same `head` syntax. Gitea then pushes the private head branch to `refs/pull/{index}/head` of the public base repository, where the public diff and patch endpoints serve it.

The related disclosure of private head repository metadata and commit SHA through `ToAPIPullRequest` in the pull request read endpoints is handled separately in https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39167.

### Impact
Confidentiality bypass of the `public-only` token boundary. A leaked public-only token can read private repository commits and diffs it was explicitly restricted from.

### Affected versions
Gitea `<= 1.27.2`.

### Patches
Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 by https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39006 and https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39013.

### Workarounds
None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.
advisories.summary: Public-only tokens can read private head repositories via compare and pull request creation (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-58443)

cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')

advisories.description: ### Summary Gitea's `diffpatch` endpoint can be abused to install and execute a Git hook from repository-controlled content. An attacker with ordinary write access to a repository can execute arbitrary shell commands as the Gitea OS user. With default open registration, an unauthenticated visitor can obtain the required write access by registering an account and creating a repository. ### Details `services/repository/files/patch.go` applies attacker-controlled patches in a shared bare temporary clone: ```go cmdApply := gitcmd.NewCommand("apply", "--index", "--recount", "--cached", "--binary") if git.DefaultFeatures().CheckVersionAtLeast("2.32") { cmdApply.AddArguments("-3") } ```` Submitting the same patch twice creates an add/add collision. Git's three-way fallback checks the indexed path out even though the operation is performed with `--cached`. In a bare clone, the repository root is `$GIT_DIR`. As a result, an executable entry named: ```text hooks/post-index-change ``` becomes a live Git hook. Git invokes the hook while writing the index, allowing repository-controlled content to execute arbitrary commands as the Gitea service account. The hook's return value is not propagated to the `diffpatch` response. The attached PoC stores command output in Git objects and creates a branch containing the result, so no outbound connection is required. The result is fetched through authenticated smart HTTP. ### PoC The supplied `gitea_diffpatch_rce_poc.py` uses an existing Gitea account. Run it against a test instance where the account can create a repository. Set the account password: ```bash export GITEA_PASSWORD='account-password' ``` Execute a command through the `diffpatch` chain: ```bash python3 ./gitea_diffpatch_rce_poc.py \ https://gitea.example \ pocuser \ 'id; uname -srm; pwd' ``` The script: * Creates an initialized private repository. * Submits the same executable-hook patch twice. * Fetches the result branch. * Prints the command's combined stdout, stderr, and exit status. * Prints the evidence repository, ref, and commit IDs to stderr. Expected output resembles: ```text uid=1000(git) gid=1000(git) groups=1000(git) Linux ... /data/gitea/tmp/... [exit-status=0] ``` The trigger requires: * Git 2.32 or newer. * An enabled `diffpatch` route. * A writable and executable temporary filesystem. Open registration is required only for the no-prior-credentials attack path. ### Impact This is remote command execution as the Gitea service account (`CWE-94`). Depending on deployment isolation and the privileges of the Gitea OS user, successful exploitation may expose: * `app.ini` and Gitea application secrets. * Process environment secrets. * Mounted repositories. * Database credentials and database contents. * OAuth and integration credentials. * Other internal or externally reachable services. advisories.description:
### Summary
An unauthenticated remote attacker can submit Org-mode markup containing
a #+INCLUDE directive to POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup for any suitable public 
repository to read arbitrary server files. By extracting INTERNAL_TOKEN from 
app.ini, they can inject a Git hook through the internal logger and achieve 
command execution as the Gitea OS user during an anonymous clone.

### Details
Gitea registers `POST /{username}/{reponame}/markup` with optional sign-in,
repository assignment, and a repository-unit reader check. An anonymous user
passes that check for a public repository with a normal readable code unit.
The handler passes the supplied `Mode`, `Text`, and `FilePath` into Gitea's
generic markup renderer. Selecting `Mode: file` and a `.org` filename chooses
the Org-mode renderer.

Gitea 1.27.0 initializes `go-org` using `org.New()` and does not replace its
default `ReadFile` callback. In `go-org` 1.9.1, that callback is `ioutil.ReadFile`; 
`#+INCLUDE` accepts absolute paths and passes them directly to that callback.

#### Preconditions

- At least one repository is publicly readable and exposes a unit accepted by
  the repository markup route. A normal public repository with its code unit
  enabled satisfies this condition.
- Standard Gitea storage permissions allow the service user to update Gitea's
  managed global Git configuration.


### Impact
- Read arbitrary files accessible to the Gitea service user without an account.
- Submit the file-read payload directly through a public repository's web markup 
   route without committing a file or obtaining repository write access.
- Expose Gitea configuration, internal bearer tokens, OAuth/JWT material, and deployment metadata

### Affected
 - The vulnerable version seem v1.22.1 ~ v1.27.0

### Credit

Found by @xbow-security. Triaged by Guido Leo <guido.leo@xbow.com>.

Independently reported by https://github.com/NightRang3r
advisories.summary: Unauthenticated Arbitrary File Read can lead to RCE

advisories.description:
### Summary
In Gitea 1.26.1, anonymous users can download draft release assets through `/attachments/{uuid}` even when the draft release itself is hidden. The generic attachment route does not re-apply the draft-release visibility check before serving the file.

### Details
The verified report ties this to `routers/web/repo/attachment.go:141-173`, which serves linked attachments without reloading the parent release or enforcing the draft flag again. `routers/api/v1/repo/release_attachment.go:23-40,134-150` shows the normal release path does enforce `canAccessReleaseDraft(ctx)`, while `services/repository/repository.go:199-204` collapses release attachments down to `unit.TypeReleases` and loses the `IsDraft` context. `routers/web/web.go:872,1471` routes UUID-based attachment downloads to the generic handler. In the verified test, anonymous access to the draft release API returned `404`, but anonymous access to `/attachments/{uuid}` returned `200` and served the draft asset content.

### PoC
1. Start an isolated Gitea 1.26.1 instance and set `BASE=http://127.0.0.1:3000`. Create a test user `owner`.
2. As `owner`, create a public initialized repository:
   `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"draft-asset-demo","private":false,"auto_init":true}' "$BASE/api/v1/user/repos"`
3. As `owner`, create a draft release and copy the returned numeric release ID:
   `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tag_name":"draft-1","name":"draft-1","draft":true}' "$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases"`
4. Create a harmless asset with recognizable content:
   `printf 'draft-only-binary' > /tmp/draft-asset.txt`
5. Upload it to the draft release and copy the returned `uuid` or `browser_download_url`:
   `curl -u owner:ownerpass123 -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/octet-stream' --data-binary @/tmp/draft-asset.txt "$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID/assets?name=draft-asset.txt"`
6. As an anonymous user with no cookies, verify the draft release itself is hidden:
   `curl -i "$BASE/api/v1/repos/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/$RELEASE_ID"`
7. Confirm this returns `404`.
8. As the same anonymous user, request the generic attachment route:
   `curl -i "$BASE/attachments/$UUID"`
9. Observe `200 OK` and the file body `draft-only-binary`.
10. Optionally compare with the normal release download route `/owner/draft-asset-demo/releases/download/draft-1/draft-asset.txt`, which should remain hidden while `/attachments/$UUID` succeeds.

### Impact
This leaks unpublished release assets. Anyone who learns the attachment UUID can retrieve draft binaries or other release files before the maintainer chooses to publish them.
advisories.summary: Generic attachment downloads bypass draft-release visibility checks
